citation: Carolwood 707 I, LLC v. Multacom Corp., No. 26STCV11606 (Cal. Super. Ct. filed Apr. 10, 2026).
forum: Superior Court of Los Angeles County
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: This is a complaint for breach of lease. The plaintiffs (CAROLWOOD 707 I, LLC & CAROLWOOD 707 II, LLC) are owners of a high-rise office building called the Aon Center in LA. Defendant MULTACOM CORPORATION leased space at the property owned by the plaintiff starting in 2006. The defendant, as the tenant, was required to pay base rent, pro rata share, utilities, etc. The tenant increased the amount of space they were renting from the plaintiff in 2014. The plaintiff’s first cause of action is breach of the written lease; the second cause of action is declaratory relief. shortName: Blocktree Properties LLC v. Public Utility District No. 2 of Grant Cnty. Washington
citation:
Blocktree Prop. L.L.C. v. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 2 of Grant Cnty. Wash., 447 F. Supp. 3d 1030 
(E.D. Wash. 2020).
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: On December 19, 2018, Cryptocurrency miners from various firms (“Plaintiffs”) based in Grant County, Washington, filed suit against Public Utility District No. 2 of Grant County, Washington (“Utility”) in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington. In response to increased requests to obtain power from the Utility by additional cryptocurrency operations, the Utility enacted Rate Schedule 17 and a corresponding new customer class, “evolving industries.” Plaintiffs fell within the evolving industries class and were subject to the new rate schedule. Plaintiffs subsequently filed suit, challenging the new rate schedule. Plaintiffs sought injunctive relief, a declaratory judgment, damages, and attorney’s fees against the Utility under federal and state law. Plaintiffs argued a violation of the Commerce Clause and the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment of the United States Constitution. Plaintiffs also claimed that the Utility created an unfair and discriminatory rate schedule and therefore violated section 20 of the Federal Power Act. Additionally, Plaintiffs argued that the Utility violated Washington ratemaking law, the Due Process Clause of the Washington State Constitution, and the Privileges and Immunities Clause of the Washington State Constitution. On March 19, 2019, the Court dismissed the Plaintiffs’ claims and ruled in favor of the Defendants. On interlocutory appeal, the Ninth Circuit affirmed this Court’s decision in an unpublished opinion.

The ballot measure created a regulatory framework for data centers and a private right of action for neighbors to data centers. The ordinance was drafted in response to an Amazon data center development proposal. The Ohio Supreme court denied the writ of mandamus because it was not within the municipality's power to enact should it pass.

citation: Nat’l Ass’n for the Advancement of Colored People v. X.AI Corp., No. 3:26-cv-00074-DMB-JMV (N.D. Miss. filed Apr. 14, 2026).

category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People sued X.AI in the Northern District of Mississippi. They brought suit under the Clean Air Act, challenging X.AI's use of gas turbines for its data centers without Clean Air Act permits, violating standards for nitrogen oxides (NOx) and hazardous air pollutants. The United States intervened with a motion to dismiss the case, and XAI filed its own motion to dismiss. The court denied XAI's motion to dismiss based on claims that the generators were mobile sources and the plaintiff's lack of standing on October 30, 2026. The United States' motion to dismiss was denied on October 19, 2026, and the 5th Circuit declined the United States' request to stay the decision. The case is ongoing.

shortName: Hoosier Environmental Council, Inc. v. Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Comm'n
citation: Hoosier Env't Council, Inc. v. Indianapolis Metro. Dev. Comm'n, No. 49D06-2605-PL-024589 (Ind. Super. Ct. Marion Cnty. filed May 1, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: The Hoosier Environmental Council and five people who live in or own homes near 25th Street and Sherman Drive filed this suit on May 1, 2026. The defendants are the developer Metrobloks, the Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission, and Sherman Investments, LLC. The suit challenges the commission's April 1, 2026 approval for a $500 million, 75-megawatt data center on ~14 acres. The site is a vacant lot that was once a drive-in movie theater. The approval included variances for 70-foot-tall buildings and changes to parking and setback requirements. The plaintiffs make several legal arguments. First, they argue that the commission did not properly apply the legal standards for granting variances. Second, they argue that the approval should not have been granted because Metrobloks did not do adequate studies of environmental impact, water use, utility use, and traffic. Third, they argue that the commission did not adequately consider the harm the project could cause to the environment, public health, and quality of life. Much of the complaint focuses on environmental justice. The neighborhood is mostly black and has a history of industrial pollution, including lead contamination, and the suit says the commission failed to consider environmental justice at all. The plaintiffs also argue that the project conflicts with the neighborhood's city-certified quality-of-life plan, which names environmental justice as a key principle. They further allege that the site's history of industrial pollution creates a risk of groundwater contamination. In support, they cite testimony about noise, air quality, water use, brownfield contamination, cumulative impacts, and inadequate environmental review. The plaintiffs ask the court to declare the approval invalid. They also seek an injunction that would bar Metrobloks from starting any construction on the project. Metrobloks has pointed to commitments it made to reduce the project's impacts, including low-emission generators that would be tested only 20 to 30 hours a year and a closed-loop cooling system. The case remains active.

shortName: Ashland Hospital Corp. v. Affiliated FM Insurance Co.
citation: Ashland Hosp. Corp. v. Affiliated FM Ins. Co., No. 0:11-cv-00016-DLB-EBA (E.D. Ky. filed Feb. 22, 2011).
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: On February 22, 2011, Ashland Hospital Corporation (“Ashland”) filed suit against Affiliated FM Insurance Company (“Affiliated FM”) in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky. After an air conditioning unit in Ashland’s data center failed, resulting in a critical computer network overheating, Ashland filed an insurance claim under Ashland’s “all risk” policy with Affiliated FM. Affiliated FM denied coverage to Ashland, and Ashland subsequently filed this lawsuit. Ashland claimed that the damage to the storage network constituted “direct physical loss or damage” under the policy and sought declaratory judgment from the court. On August 14, 2013, the Court held that the overheating caused a physical alteration to the data storage components themselves and that the phrase “direct and physical loss or damage” includes a loss of reliability suffered by a data storage network due to heat exposure. Thus, the court granted Ashland’s motion for declaratory judgment as to coverage under the policy.

citation: Pacheco v. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs of Doña Ana Cnty., No. D-307-CV-2025-02764 (N.M. Dist. Ct. filed Oct. 17, 2025).

category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: On October 17, 2025, Petitioner Derrick Pacheco filed a petition for judicial review against the Board of County Commissioners of Dona Ana County in New Mexico's 3rd Judicial District Court. The petition challenges the Board's approval of an ordinance, which authorized $165 billion in industrial revenue bonds for Project Jupiter (a data center campus for Oracle and OpenAI in Santa Teresa). Pacheco claims the Board acted improperly by approving the bonds while the project's land-use approval was still pending before the County Planning and Zoning Commission, and despite documents missing from the commissioners' packets. He asked the court to reverse or vacate the decision. The Judge has dismissed the petition twice without prejudice for pleading defects, most recently on Jun. 23, 2026, which gave Pacheco one more chance to file an amended petition. Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International sued under the Clean Air Act and the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act. EPA reconsidered and extended the compliance timeline for hydrofluorocarbons in industrial chillers while the litigation was pending. In June 2026, the D.C. Circuit dismissed the lawsuit.

shortName: In re Interconnection & Tariffs for Large Load Customers
citation: In re Interconnection & Tariffs for Large Load Customers, No. M-2025-3054271 (Pa. Pub. Util. Comm'n May 12, 2026) (final order).
summary: On April 12, 2025, the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission issued a notice initiating an administrative proceeding concerning interconnection and tariff requirements for large electricity customers, including data centers. The proceeding involves state public utility ratemaking, interconnection regulation, cost allocation, financial assurances, and federal jurisdiction over transmission infrastructure. Electric utilities, technology companies, industry associations, environmental organizations, and consumer advocacy groups submitted testimony and comments. On May 12, 2026, the Commission issued a final order establishing a model large-load tariff addressing contract terms, financial security, infrastructure costs, and interconnection procedures. The Energy Association of Pennsylvania subsequently petitioned for reconsideration or clarification, raising concerns regarding federal jurisdiction over transmission upgrades and interconnection studies, but withdrew its petition on June 1, 2026. On July 16, 2026, the Commission granted the withdrawal and formally closed the proceeding.

shortName: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC vs. Imperial Irrigation District
citation: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC vs. Imperial Irrigation District
category: Environmental Law: Water Rights and Usage
summary: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing (IVCM) sued the Imperial Irrigation District (IID) after IID denied IVCM's April 22, 2026 application for industrial water service, seeking roughly 260–287 million gallons (about 880 acre-feet) of Colorado River water annually to cool its proposed 330-megawatt AI data center. IVCM alleges IID broke its own rules by denying an industrial applicant the right to combine water rights from contiguous, commonly-owned parcels — a "farm unit" consolidation IID routinely permits for agricultural users — and contends there is "no rational basis" for IID to treat industrial and agricultural water-reallocation requests differently. IVCM describes the request as a "last resort" after months of failed negotiations for recycled wastewater with the cities of El Centro and Imperial, and says the request represents a small fraction (roughly 0.03%) of IID's total Colorado River allocation; the suit asks the court to order IID to reconsider or approve the water-service application.

category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: On January 9, 2026, Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC filed a lawsuit in the United States District Court, Southern District of California, against the City of Imperial and four city officials. The plaintiff brings civil rights claims including: (1) Violation of Procedural Due Process, (2) First Amendment Retaliation, (3) Equal Protection Class of One Claim, and (4) Municipal Liability (Monell). The plaintiff alleges that the defendants obstructed applications for its proposed $10 billion AI data center and retaliated against it after it relocated the data center to Imperial County. The plaintiff seeks compensatory damages for alleged direct delay costs, unnecessary design expenses, and lost business opportunities, including damages against the City estimated to exceed $1 million, and cost of suit and reasonable attorneys' fees. On May 29, 2026, the court denied the plaintiff's request for an Early Neutral Evaluation conference ("ENE"), a discovery conference, and/or a status/case management conference while the defendants’ motion to dismiss remained pending. The case remains open, and no final decision appears in the available docket.

summary: George McNerney and four other Fort Meade, Florida residents — organized as the "Watchdogs of Fort Meade" — filed two lawsuits on May 14, 2026 against the City of Fort Meade after its City Commission voted 5-0 on April 14, 2026 to approve a 20-year development agreement for a $2.6 billion, 4.4-million-square-foot Stonebridge hyperscale AI data center campus on a 1,300-acre former phosphate mine, despite 40 of 41 public commenters speaking in opposition. One suit, a petition for writ of certiorari, alleges the city failed to properly notify residents of key hearings held in 2025 and never adequately reviewed whether the project was compatible with the surrounding neighborhood before approval; the Florida Department of Commerce separately called the city's review "fundamentally flawed" and criticized the developer's water-demand estimates as significantly understated. citation: Greene et al. v. Nebius Inc. et al

Plaintiffs allege the city allowed the project to proceed without required zoning approvals or public hearings, contending the site's mixed-use zoning does not permit a hyperscale facility and that any "grandfathered" development rights tied to a prior building on the site were lost when that building was demolished. The suit further challenges the adequacy of approval for a proposed power substation and switching station — which failed to receive enough votes from the city's Zoning Board of Adjustment in March 2026 — and an internal city attorney memo the plaintiffs say improperly tried to override that board's action; plaintiffs seek to halt construction and recover damages for property values and quality of life.

shortName: Andrew Frank v. Coshocton County Port Authority
citation: Frank v. Coshocton Cnty. Port Auth., No. 2026-00623PQ (Ohio Ct. Cl. filed June 30, 2026).
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: On July 24, 2025, Aligned Data Centers announced a 197-acre data center campus inside the Conesville Industrial Park, next to the former AEP Conesville Power Plant. On May 26, 2026, Andrew Frank made a public records request to the Coshocton County Port Authority about the Aligned Data Centers project, going back to October 1, 2024. Frank’s request for lease applications, engineering and allocation records, and meeting minutes was granted; however, the port authority asked him to narrow his request for emails, texts, letters, and other correspondence of Executive Director Tiffany Swigert and the board members containing keywords like “Aligned,” “Frontier,” and “Conesville,” and he limited it to accounts belonging to Swigert and sitting board members. The port authority’s attorney said the request did not allow for an adequate search and there was not enough clarity on who sent and received the emails. On June 17, 2026, Frank filed a public records complaint under Ohio’s Public Records Act with the Coshocton County Clerk, which the Ohio Court of Claims received on June 30, 2026. On July 1, 2026, the court appointed a special master and referred the complaint to mediation.

shortName: In re Public Utility Comm'n of Oregon (Investigation into Marginal Cost Study Treatment)
citation: In re Investigation into Marginal Cost Study Treatment of Costs for Large Customers & Further Modifications to Portland Gen. Elec. Co.'s Rule C & Rule I, No. UM 2377 (Or. Pub. Util. Comm'n May 7, 2026) (Order No. 26-154).
summary: On March 7, 2025, the Public Utility Commission of Oregon initiated an investigation into how Portland General Electric Company charges large electricity customers, particularly data centers, for the infrastructure and services needed to meet their energy demands. The proceeding addresses utility ratemaking, transmission and interconnection cost allocation, and implementation of Oregon's 2025 POWER Act, which requires a separate service classification for large data centers. Portland General Electric, Amazon Data Services, the Data Center Coalition, industrial customers, consumer advocates, and environmental and community organizations participated in the contested proceeding. On May 7, 2026, the Commission issued Order No. 26-154, establishing Schedule 96 for data centers of 20 megawatts or more, with minimum payment requirements, long-term contracts, exit fees, protections against shifting costs to other customers, and an interconnection queue tied to clean-energy requirements. Order No. 26-239, entered July 10, 2026, approved implementing tariffs, while Order No. 26-309, entered August 31, 2026, partly granted and partly denied requests for reconsideration, rehearing, and clarification. On September 10, 2026, the Alliance of Western Energy Consumers petitioned the Oregon Court of Appeals for judicial review of all three orders, while Portland General Electric submitted a further compliance filing on September 15, 2026. The Commission's decisions governing data center electricity rates and service requirements are active. The final legal status of these decisions is pending due to the subsequent appeals.

LBT purchased a property from Sugarloaf Township in December 2024. The record owner of this property is the Richard E Angelo Family Limited Partnership. Sugarloaf Township informed LBT that they would “not consider nor adopt” LBT’s request for a Curative Amendment to the Ordinances that would allow for data centers. The plaintiff, who has made a financial investment to build a data center in Hill County, claims that this moratorium is illegal and that the defendants had no legal authority to proceed with it. summary: The petition was filed in Carroll County Superior Court on Feb. 10, 2025. The petitioners are 11 named residents, led by Dylan Cook, plus "John and Jane Does 1-20". The petitioners describe themselves as adjacent and nearby landowners in Carroll County and Villa Rica. The respondents are the City of Villa Rica; Embry Development Company, LLC; Avemore GA, LLC; Artesia Capital, LLC; and Jerry C. Tolbert. The plaintiffs challenge alleged actions by the City of Villa Rica, the Embry Development Company and another property owner regarding more than 200 acres of land between Hickory Level Road and South Van Wert Road. The petitioners challenge the City Council's Jan. 14, 2025 votes annexing two parcels out of unincorporated Carroll County and rezoning three parcels for a data center project. They ask the court to declare the annexation and rezoning actions void. The petition seeks judicial review under O.C.G.A. § 5-3-1 and O.C.G.A. § 36-66-5.1, and cites the Development of Regional Impact rules, Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 110-12-3. The petition relies on the zoning notice requirements of O.C.G.A. § 36-66-4 and invokes annexation statutes on carve-outs and unincorporated "islands," O.C.G.A. §§ 36-36-20(a)(2) and 36-36-4(a). It also cites the statutory rule on the order of annexation and rezoning votes, O.C.G.A. § 36-36-4(d). The remaining claims rest on city application requirements and on whether the applicant was authorized to file. On May 13, 2025, the council approved annexation and rezoning again on a new application for the same property while the case was pending. The case is ongoing.

The proceeding concerns utility certification, resource planning, procurement requirements, and allocation of infrastructure costs associated with large electricity loads. Environmental and consumer advocates, industrial customers, electric cooperatives, and Meta participated, with opponents questioning the need for three proposed gas-fired generating units, supporting evidence, contractual transparency, and potential costs to existing ratepayers. corporateEntities: Vantage Data Center "Lighthouse"; Open AI; Oracle
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: On January 29, 2026, a group of Wisconsin construction, real estate, and commerce associations, alongside Sids Sealants LLC and Sid Arthur, sued the City of Port Washington in the Ozaukee County Circuit Court over a citizen initiative. This initiative for the April 2026 ballot would require voter approval prior to the creation or approval of any Tax Incremental District (TID) for any project with a projected base property value or projected cost of $10 million or more. The initiative was created in response to the Port Washington City Council’s approval of the development agreement for a proposed $15 billion Vantage data center campus. Initially, in February, the plaintiffs filed a motion for a temporary restraining order and temporary injunction blocking the initiative from the ballot. Great Lakes Neighbors United, which proposed the initiative, joined as an intervenor against the plaintiffs’ motion. The court denied the motion for an injunction at the end of February, and the initiative passed on the April ballot. The plaintiffs then filed for summary judgment in July, asking for declaratory judgment on the basis that the initiative contradicted state law, which already laid out a TID approval process. On October 19, 2026, the court gave an oral ruling denying the plaintiffs' summary judgment and granting declaratory judgment in favor of the defendant.

forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: Plaintiff Atlas provides commercial and industrial installation services. Defendant I2G provides installation and maintenance of security services for large, complex, high-value facilities. I2G contracted with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to maintain their Licking County, Ohio, data server facility security. I2G asked Atlas for a quote to install security system wiring at the AWS facility. AWS asked I2G to have Atlas employees present on site at all times for miscellaneous standby work. I2G paid Atlas 89,999 for standby work in March 2018. Atlas issued three invoices to I2G for August, October, and December 2018 standby work totalling $139,609.20. I2G did not pay this sum, nor did it pay $177,686.50 for non-standby work. Atlas stopped working at the facility in April 2019. Both sides sued each other for breach of contract. Plaintiff sued for unjust enrichment and sought a declaratory judgment. I2G claims tortious interference with contract, tortious interference with a business relationship, and civil conspiracy to harm I2G's business relationships with AWS. The court grants in part and denies in part the Plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment. Court grants in part and denies in part the Defendant’s motion for sanctions.

shortName: Maryland Office of People's Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, LLC
citation: Maryland Office of People’s Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, LLC
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: The Maryland Office of People's Counsel (OPC), which represents Maryland utility ratepayers, filed a complaint with FERC on May 7, 2026 alleging that PJM Interconnection's "hybrid" methodology for allocating the costs of regional high-voltage transmission projects violates the Federal Power Act by unfairly shifting data-center-driven infrastructure costs onto Maryland customers. OPC's complaint, supported by an expert affidavit, alleges that of $22 billion in transmission project costs PJM has advanced over the past three years — overwhelmingly to meet data center demand concentrated in states like Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Illinois — PJM's rules have assigned Maryland customers (mostly served by Baltimore Gas and Electric and Pepco) roughly $2 billion in capital costs that will add an estimated $1.6 billion to Maryland electric bills over the next decade, despite Maryland's comparatively modest data-center-driven load growth. OPC asks FERC to require PJM to assign data-center-driven transmission costs to the specific PJM zones where the data centers are located, or alternatively to charge those costs directly to the large data center customers themselves, consistent with a "Ratepayer Protection Pledge" signed by hyperscale developers at the White House on March 4, 2026.

summary: Meta is developing an approximately $1 billion data center in Beaver Dam spanning 700,000 square feet. summary: Plaintiff (Navigators Specialty Insurance Company) brings this suit against Defendant (SVO Building One LLC) saying that it is entitled to reimbursement of all defense fees and costs incurred in previous litigation (Liebert Corporation v. SVO Building One, LLC - Case No. 01-18-0003-1318). Plaintiff is attempting to recover fees paid during the defense process of uncovered claims, but does not seek reimbursement of attorney’s fees/costs incurred in SVO’s defense of claims covered under the Policy. The Policy was issued to SVO from July 12, 2017 to Aug 12, 2019, and is a business description for an “8 Month OCP Data Center Construction Project”. The Policy only allows for Commercial General Liability coverage on the bounds of the property itself. In the Liebert case, claimant Liebert Corporation filed a claim that Liebert was in an agreement with SVO to design and construct a data center at the property site. Liebert’s agreement said that it would maintain ownership of IP and work product in the construction of the data center and that SVO had a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, revocable license to use Liebert’s IP and work product only in connection with this particular site. SVO terminated the contract with Liebert after Phase 1 of construction and according to Liebert, wrongfully disclosed trade secret information and patented tech with Liebert’s competitors. shortName: Keep It Rural LLC v. Columbus Council
citation: Keep It Rural LLC v. City of Columbus, No. SU2026CV001406 (Ga. Super. Ct. Muscogee Cnty. filed June 22, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Keep It Rural, LLC and eight landowners filed the suit in Muscogee County Superior Court. The eight landowners are Stacie Mailey, Debbie Jackson, Charles McClure, Jeremy Gibson, Jordan Kempson, Robert Landi, Wayne Gasser, and Debra Jarzomkowski. They live near the roughly 865-acre site proposed for "Project Ruby," a planned data center with an estimated cost of $5.18 billion. The defendants are the City of Columbus, Mayor B.H. "Skip" Henderson III, and all 10 members of the city council. The suit challenges Ordinance No. 26-034, a "Technology Overlay District" law. The council passed it on June 16, 2026. The ordinance allows large data centers on sites of 75 acres or more on land now zoned for farming and rural homes. The claims rely on five main sources of law: 1) The Georgia Zoning Procedures Law: The plaintiffs say the council changed the ordinance after the public hearing and then passed it without a new hearing. 2) The city's own rules, meaning the Columbus Unified Development Ordinance and the city charter. 3) Due process under the U.S. and Georgia Constitutions: The plaintiffs say they did not get fair notice or a real chance to be heard. 4) The Georgia Open Meetings Act: The plaintiffs say the review committee met in private five times. 5) Georgia zoning-power limits: The plaintiffs say the ordinance is arbitrary, is "spot zoning" written for one project, and leaves key decisions to private development agreements. The plaintiffs want the court to declare the ordinance void and unenforceable and have asked for a temporary restraining order and a permanent injunction. These actions would stop the city from accepting or processing applications under the ordinance, including one for Project Ruby. They are asking the court to send the ordinance back to the council to redo the process and want their legal costs and attorney fees paid. The city's response is that the ordinance does not rezone any land or approve any data center. The city says it only sets up a process for future applications, and no application has been filed. On Aug. 7 the city asked the court to dismiss all seven counts and listed 15 defenses. The judge has not ruled on the motion to dismiss yet.

summary: Plaintiff Vertical Bridge is a telecommunications infrastructure company (including cellular communication and television/radio broadcast towers). Defendant is Everest, VB’s direct competitor in the telecommunications infrastructure industry. Plaintiff claims that Everest has developed and implemented an improper, multi-state, and multi-million-dollar scheme to unlawfully improve its market share at Vertical Bridge’s expense through trade secret misappropriation, false advertising, tortious interference with contract, and unfair competition. The plaintiff’s causes of action include: 1. False advertising under the Lanham Act (claim that Everest makes false and/or misleading statements of fact regarding the nature of the services and commercial activities of Vertical Bridge); 2. Federal Defend Trade Secrets Act claim (Vertical Bridge uses trade secret pricing information to enter into contracts across the country) 3. Pennsylvania Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Vertical Bridge's confidential information is entitled to trade secret protection) 4. Unjust Enrichment (Everest has acquired multiple VB contracts containing confidential price terms/price structure info) 5. Tortious interference with existing contractual relations 6. Tortious interference with prospective contractual relations 7. Unfair Competition (claim that Everest engages in unfair/deceptive business practices). The case was ultimately dismissed.

Ultimately, rather than proceeding through full litigation or a contested hearing, the matter reached a final resolution when the parties filed a joint stipulation to dismiss the case with prejudice, which was formally ordered and closed by Judge Steven M. Cain on October 16, 2026.

summary: Plaintiffs successfully placed a proposed city ordinance against a data center on the county ballot. The city responded with a suit challenging the ordinance as administrative, rather than legislative. A Johnson County judge granted the plaintiff's mortion to strike the city’s lawsuit against two residents for violating their rights under the Kansas Public Speech Protection Act and ruled the city must pay the plaintiff's attorney's fees.

shortName: South Carolina Public Interest Foundation v. Dorchester Cnty.
citation: S.C. Pub. Int. Found. v. Dorchester Cnty., No. 2024-CP-18-00518 (S.C. Ct. C.P. Dorchester Cnty. filed Apr. 11, 2024).
forum: South Carolina Court of Common Pleas
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: The county redacted the projected water and sewer usage for Google’s planned data center near St. George from public record after Google stated the information was a trade secret. In September 2023, the county rejected Frank Heindel’s request for this water usage information under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act. In April 2024, a lawsuit was filed against Dorchester County in the Dorchester County Court of Common Pleas by the South Carolina Public Interest Foundation, which is overseen by Frank Heindel. The plaintiffs claimed that the county violated the state’s open-records act because Google’s water usage was not a trade secret, and asked the court to require the county to disclose this information. Around January 2025, the county settled, agreeing that Google’s water usage was not a trade secret and to make Google’s daily and monthly water usage public at the St. George data center, because of the county’s special water services agreement there.

shortName: In re Archer Datacenters Environmental Assessment Worksheet
citation: In re Approving the Findings of Fact & Record of Decision for Archer Datacenters Env't Assessment Worksheet, No. A25-1617, slip op. (Minn. Ct. App. June 8, 2026).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy ("MCEA") appealed the City of Faribault's determination that a proposed Archer Datacenters project did not require a full environmental impact statement. MCEA argued that the city's environmental review inadequately assessed air quality, noise pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and cumulative environmental impacts. On June 8, 2026, the Minnesota Court of Appeals reversed the city's determination and found that its conclusions were unsupported by substantial evidence. The court also rejected the city's attempt to defer further environmental analysis until later stages. The case was remanded, requiring the city to either make a positive declaration requiring an environmental impact statement or postpone its decision.

category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: A coalition of electrical utilities called the Grid Acceleration Coalition ("the Coalition"), including Xcel Energy and American Transmission Company and others, filed a complaint with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ("FERC") on April 7, 2026 against the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. ("MISO") and the Southwest Power Pool, Inc. ("SPP"). The Coalition seeks an order finding that the solicitation processes for certain regional transmission projects under the MISO and SPP Tariffs are unjust and unreasonable under the Federal Power Act due to the delays the processes cause. The Coalition instead seeks fast-track processing, but does not seek a shortened comment period. The matter is pending as of October 2026.

shortName: The nonprofit group Joliet Residents for Responsible Growth, along with individual local residents, filed suit against the City of Joliet and developers to block the approval of the Joliet Technology Center data center project. The group is challenging the annexation and rezoning of 795 acres for a $20 billion data center project. The city calls voiding the vote too extreme of a remedy. The case is ongoing.
citation: Joliet Residents for Responsible Growth v. City of Joliet, No. 2026CH000108 (Ill. Cir. Ct. filed May 18, 2026).
corporateEntities: Powerhouse Hillwood Holding, LLC; HW Technology Park Development, LLC; American Real Estate Partners; City of Joliet.
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Joliet Residents for Responsible Growth, along with three individual plaintiffs living near the proposed site, sued the City of Joliet and developers Powerhouse Hillwood Holding, HW Technology Park Development, and American Real Estate Partners, challenging the City Council's March 19, 2026 approval (by an 8-1 vote) of an annexation agreement for the $20 billion, 795-acre "Joliet Technology Center" data center campus. The suit alleges the city's February 18 public notice for the Plan Commission hearing failed to disclose that the project involved a 24-building, 1.8-gigawatt data center as required by Illinois law; that a March 19 special council meeting violated the Open Meetings Act by not occurring within 24 hours of a prior meeting with an unchanged agenda; that residents were denied due process, including the right to cross-examine developer witnesses; and that rezoning the land from agricultural to light industrial is unconstitutional because it bears no substantial relation to public health, safety, or welfare. The suit also alleges a conflict of interest because the city's planning director is the daughter of a person with a financial stake in the project, and asks the court to void the City Council's approval.

shortName: McNerney,  et al. v. City of Fort Meade
citation: McNerney,  et al. v. City of Fort Meade
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: George McNerney and four other Fort Meade, Florida residents — organized as the "Watchdogs of Fort Meade" — filed two lawsuits on May 14, 2026 against the City of Fort Meade after its City Commission voted 5-0 on April 14, 2026 to approve a 20-year development agreement for a $2.6 billion, 4.4-million-square-foot Stonebridge hyperscale AI data center campus on a 1,300-acre former phosphate mine, despite 40 of 41 public commenters speaking in opposition. One suit, a petition for writ of certiorari, alleges the city failed to properly notify residents of key hearings held in 2025 and never adequately reviewed whether the project was compatible with the surrounding neighborhood before approval; the Florida Department of Commerce separately called the city's review "fundamentally flawed" and criticized the developer's water-demand estimates as significantly understated. Plaintiffs ask the court to void the city's approval; they have also launched a recall campaign against three city commissioners.

shortName: Coalition for Responsible Data Center Development v. City of Farmington
citation: Coal. for Responsible Data Ctr. Dev. v. City of Farmington, No. 19HA-CV-24-5838 (Minn. Dist. Ct. Dakota Cnty. Sept. 4, 2026) (dismissed with prejudice).
corporateEntities: Tract; MNLCO Farmington LLC; MNLCO Farmington Two LLC
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: A residents' group, the Coalition for Responsible Data Center Development, sued Farmington in November 2024. The suit targets the planned unit development the city approved in December 2024. Castle Rock Township filed its own suit in 2025, and the two cases were consolidated. The township's claims centered on breach of the orderly annexation agreement. The court denied the city's motion to dismiss the Coalition's suit on May 27, 2025. In September 2026 the Coalition withdrew, citing litigation costs. The court dismissed all five of the Coalition's counts with prejudice on September 4, 2026. Castle Rock's suit was dismissed with prejudice on September 15, 2026.

shortName: Ostergaard v. Microsoft Corp.
citation: Ostergaard v. Microsoft Corp., No. 2:26-cv-01169 (E.D. Wis. filed July 1, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin
category: Common Law: Property
summary: On July 1, 2026, Garret Ostergaard, David Wade, and Joy Wade, on behalf of themselves and all others similarly situated, filed a proposed class-action lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin, against Microsoft Corporation, which operates and maintains the data center located at 4800 90th Street, Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin 53403 ("Data Center"). The plaintiffs brought claims for private nuisance and negligence, alleging that the Data Center emitted unreasonable and excessive noise that interfered with their use and enjoyment of their properties and reduced their property values. The plaintiffs sought class certification, designation as class representatives and designation of their counsel as class counsel, judgment in their favor, compensatory and exemplary damages, pre-judgment and post-judgment interest, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief not inconsistent with the defendant's local, state, and federal regulatory obligations. On September 22, 2026, the parties notified the court that they had agreed on the material terms of a settlement in principle and jointly requested a stay while they finalized the settlement agreement. On September 23, 2026, the court granted the stay and directed the parties to file a motion for preliminary approval or an updated status report by November 2, 2026. The case remains open, and no final decision appears in the available docket.

category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Petitioner is a Sugar Grove Resident who filed suit against Pioneer Development LLC and Yorkville officials to challenge the city's approval of a proposed 1037-acre data center campus ("Project Cardinal"). Plaintiffs sought to overturn the project's rezoning and argued that the development would negatively affect nearby property values and residents' quality of life. The parties reached a conditional settlement in June 2026.

shortName: 406 People First and Denise Kelly vs. The City-County of Buttesilver Bow and Cynthia Sherman, in her official capacity as Clerk and Recorder/Election Administrator
citation: 406 People First v. County of Butte-Silver Bow, No. DV-26-298-FJ (Mont. 2d Dist. Ct., Silver Bow Cnty. Aug. 28, 2026), appeal docketed, No. DA 26-0618 (Mont. Aug. 31, 2026)
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: Denise Kelly and 406 People First filed a complaint against the City-County of Buttesilver Bow and Cynthia Sherman, the Clerk and Election Administrator, on August 12, 2026 in Montana District Court Silver Bow. Kelly alleges that the Administrator notified them in writing that they had until August 14 to complete their petitions and signatures regarding Local Initiative 00-02, the Butte Data Center Initiative, for the November 3, 2026 election. However, on August 10, the Administrator said that MCA § 13-28-206 appeared to set a deadline of July 13 and retroactively disqualified petition activity after that time. Kelly sought a writ of mandamus for the Administrator to certify the Initiative, declaratory judgment that the August 14 deadline should be honored, equitable and statutory estoppel from rejecting signatures as untimely, and enjoinment from destroying any petitions or withholding certification. Injunctive relief was denied on August 28. On August 31, 2026, 406 People First and Kelly filed an appeal with the Supreme Court of Montana. Injunctive relief was granted on September 22, 2026 and then vacated on September 24, 2026 after the Court was informed that the election ballots had already been mailed out and some had already been returned. 406 People First then filed an emergency petition for rehearing which was denied on September 25 for not demonstrating exceptional circumstances that warranted a rehearing. The appeal is ongoing as of October 2026.

shortName: Curtis v. City of Sulphur Springs
citation: Curtis v. City of Sulphur Springs, No. CV46082 (Hopkins Cnty. Dist. Ct., Tex. filed Apr. 14, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Sulphur Springs resident Jack Curtis filed suit against the City of Sulphur Springs, Texas, alleging violations of the Texas Open Meetings Act in connection with city council deliberations over a proposed hyperscale data center project, referred to in city records as the “Matrix Project,” on the former Luminant Thermo site. Curtis contends that the City’s council agendas and meeting minutes failed to adequately disclose the nature of a letter of intent between the City and MSB Global Services and did not identify the counterparty, depriving residents of meaningful notice of the project’s terms. He seeks a declaration that the resulting agreements between the City and MSB Global Services are void. The City has continued to address this litigation, along with a related suit, in closed executive sessions under Texas Government Code Chapter 551. Available sources do not indicate that a final ruling has been issued in the case as of October 2026.

citation: Tait Electric Generating Station, LLC, No. EC26-83-000 (FERC filed Apr. 3, 2026).
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: Tait Electric Generating Station, LLC (“Tait”), Lee County Generating Station, LLC (“Lee County”), and Hull Street Energy, LLC (“HSE”) submitted an application with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) seeking authorization for a transaction pursuant to section 203(a)(1) of the Federal Power Act and Part 33 of the regulations of the FERC. The Lee County generating station is a 677 MW power plant in Dixon, Illinois. In the transaction, GridFlex Generation HoldCo, LLC (“Seller”) will sell one hundred percent of the ownership interest in GridFlex Generation, LLC (“Company”) to MPH GridFlex, LLC (“MPH”). The Company owns one hundred percent of Tait and Lee County, and MPH is owned by affiliates of HSE. Thus, following the completion of the transaction, Tait and Lee will be indirect wholly-owned subsidiaries of MPH. On August 13, 2026, FERC issued an order authorizing the Proposed Transaction under FERC’s Merger Policy Statement and determined the transaction as consistent with the public interest.

shortName: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
citation: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
forum: "District Court of Texas, 419th Judicial District, Travis County"
category: Constitutional Law: Takings
summary: Data Foundry, Inc., an internet service provider operating data centers in Austin, sued the City of Austin over rates charged by Austin Energy, the city-owned electric utility, alleging the rates are unjust, unreasonable, excessive, confiscatory, discriminatory, and constitute a taking. The trial court dismissed Data Foundry's claims for lack of standing; the Fourteenth Court of Appeals held Data Foundry had standing but still affirmed dismissal of the claims on other grounds. On April 9, 2021, the Texas Supreme Court held that Data Foundry has standing as a ratepayer to challenge generally applicable municipal utility rates without needing to show an injury distinct from other ratepayers, reversed the courts below in part, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings on the merits of the rate challenge.

category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: On Nov 24, 2025, the Archbald Borough Council approved a zoning overlay allowing data centers in a region currently zoned for conservation and residential use. On December 23, 2025, Archbald residents Phillip Sardo, Jack and Amy Swingle, Marilyn Jones, Robert and Phyliss Paone, Joseph Sabia and Justin Healey filed a land use appeal in the Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas, Lackawanna County, claiming that the process to approve the data center zoning amendment was not completed in accordance with the procedural requirements in the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code. They are seeking to have the court invalidate the amendment. The case is ongoing as of October 2026.

shortName: Gonzalez v. Holland
citation: Gonzalez v. Holland, No. 2616-CV08337 (Mo. Cir. Ct. Jackson Cnty. Mar. 25, 2026).
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: In early March 2026, the Independence City Council approved more than $6 billion in tax breaks for Nebius, a Dutch company building a 400-plus-acre “AI factory.” After this vote, residents started a petition for a referendum to put the tax breaks up to a citywide vote, and the city rejected the effort. On March 9, 2026, Rachel Gonzalez, Kharma Magers, and Misty Vaughn, three residents who supported the referendum, filed suit in the Jackson County Circuit Court against Susanne Holland, Independence City Clerk, and the City of Independence. The city argued that the city’s charter did not allow a referendum because the ordinance granting the tax breaks had already taken effect; the residents argued that the ordinance could not take effect until the referendum process had finished. On March 25, 2026, the court denied the residents’ request for declaratory judgment and entered judgment in favor of the clerk and the city.

category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Tucker United, West Virginia Highlands Conservancy, and Sierra Club appealed an air permit to the West Virginia Air Quality Board questioning whether the applicant had proper site control of the facility. The WVAQP found that the developer, Fundamental Data, met sight control requirements.

shortName: City of The Dalles v. Oregonian Publishing Co.
citation: City of The Dalles v. Oregonian Publ’g Co., No. 21CV39645 (Or. Cir. Ct. Wasco Cnty. 2022).
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: In 2021, The Dalles, Oregon, and Google negotiated an agreement to build two new data centers, in addition to the Google campus that was already along the Columbia River. As part of the deal, Google would pay $28.5 million to upgrade the city’s water supply and transfer some of its water rights to the city. However, in the public version of the agreement, the number of gallons allotted for Google’s use was removed because it was considered a trade secret, based on Google’s concern that its competitors would learn how it cools its servers. In September 2021, an Oregonian reporter requested that Google’s water usage be released as public records, but the city denied the request. The Oregonian requested a review of the denial by the Wasco County District Attorney’s office, which ordered the release of the records. In October 2021, the City of The Dalles, on behalf of Google, sued The Oregonian and its reporter, represented by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, a nonprofit group, in Wasco County Circuit Court in order to prevent the release of Google’s water usage, which the plaintiff argued was a trade secret exempt from Oregon’s public records law. In November 2021, the city council approved Google’s proposal to build two new data centers, before litigation had finished and while Google’s water usage was still not public. On November 14, 2022, the city council voted to authorize the city attorney to settle. In December 2022, a settlement was filed in which the city agreed to disclose to anyone who requested it 10 years of Google’s water usage and any future usage. Google also stated that water usage would no longer be considered a trade secret.

shortName: Allen v. City of Sydney
citation: Allen v. City of Sidney, 2026-Ohio-3403 (2026)
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: Plaintiff (Allen) filed a complaint against defendant City of Sidney alleging that she was denied access to public records about a certain data center development project. Allen claimed this was in violation of  R.C. 149.43(B) of the Ohio Revised Code. Amazon Data Services, Inc. moved to intervene in this filing, and Amazon Data Services, Inc., and the City jointly moved for leave to respond to requester’s complain. The City moved for dismissal of the claims under R.C. 2743.75(E)(2) and Civ.R. 12(B)(6). The Court found that the City of Sidney’s objections lacked merit, that Amazon's joinder was improper, and that Allen's objections lacked merit (and were thereby overruled).

shortName: National CRE Holdings LLC, et al. v. Hood Cty. Texas, et al.
citation: National CRE Holdings LLC, et al. v. Hood Cty. Texas, et al.
forum: "355th Judicial District Court of Texas, Hood County"
corporateEntities: National CRE Holdings and Greenland Capital
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: National CRE Holdings (an affiliate of Starwood Capital Group) and Greenland Capital LLC (owner of MARA Holdings) sued Hood County, arguing that the county's failure to approve or reject their proposed "Project Red" and "Project Yellow" data center concept plans within 30 days meant the projects were automatically approved under the Texas Local Government Code's "shot clock" provision. The county countered that the 30-day deadline never applied because the submitted materials did not meet the statutory definition of "development plans" requiring formal review. On July 20, 2026, Judge Bryan Bufkin dismissed the developers' lawsuit and ruled it could not be refiled in its current form, preserving the county's ability to review the projects' impacts on local water resources and infrastructure before construction; the developers have filed a notice of appeal to the Second Court of Appeals.

shortName: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC v. City of Yorkville
citation: Preserve Our Yorkville & Cmty., LLC v. City of Yorkville, No. 2026CH13 (Kendall Cnty. Cir. Ct. filed May 22, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC, and several individual and business plaintiffs, including neighboring landowners, filed suit against the City of Yorkville, Illinois, in Kendall County Circuit Court on May 22, 2026, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief. The plaintiffs challenge the city’s approval of a rezoning ordinance for a data center campus known as Project Steel, developed by Prologis, L.P., along the Eldamain Road corridor. They allege that the city denied adjacent landowners a statutory right to a fair public hearing, omitted required notice ahead of a July 2025 hearing, and violated the Illinois Open Meetings Act when the council approved the project at its March 24, 2026 meeting. The plaintiffs then contend that the rezoning conflicts with the City’s 2016 Comprehensive Plan. They seek a declaration that the rezoning ordinance is void and an order halting development pending review of its validity. Prologis, L.P. has since entered an appearance in the case, and as of October 2026, the matter remains pending, with the next status hearing scheduled for December 18, 2026.

shortName: State ex rel. Snyder v. City of Joplin
citation: State ex rel. Snyder v. City of Joplin, No. 26AO-CC00090 (Mo. Cir. Ct. Jasper Cnty. filed Mar. 17, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Plaintiffs in this case are Derek and Laura Snyder, trustees of the Snyder Trust and residents of Wildwood Ranch. They filed a petition against the City of Joplin, Mayor Keenan Cortez, and Wildwood Ranch, LLC. They filed the case in the Circuit Court of Jasper County, Missouri. They sought judicial review of the council's approval of a voluntary annexation of around 540 acres and the rezoning of around 600 acres from R-1 (single-family residential) to M-2 (heavy industrial) to accommodate a data center. Plaintiffs claim the rezoning was unreasonable and ignored relevant facts. They also claim it was approved without a site or concept plan and without the traffic, environmental, or utility studies the City's zoning code requires, and that the Council gave up its legislative and police powers by relying on a 2009 annexation agreement with the property owner. Plaintiffs ask the court to void the rezoning.

category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Greater Indiantown Community Alliance, Inc. (“GICA”), and four individual residents from Martin County, Florida filed suit against the Village of Indiantown and Florida Power & Light Company in the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit Court of Florida on May 25, 2026, alleging that the Village’s approval of the Tesoro Groves Planned Unit Development was illegal spot zoning and created an illegal enclave in violation of Florida Statute §163.3215. The plaintiffs sought a declaratory judgment as to the legality of the annexation and rezoning and a permanent injunction against the use of the land parcel for industrial purposes. The case was voluntarily dismissed with prejudice on July 2, 2026.

shortName: MCEA v. City of Monticello
citation: Minn. Ctr. for Env't Advoc. v. City of Monticello, No. 86-CV-26-1130 (Minn. Dist. Ct. filed Feb. 25, 2026).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: On February 25, 2026, the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy (MCEA) initiated a civil lawsuit in Wright County District Court against the City of Monticello and developer Monticello Tech LLC. On the basis of Minnesota environmental review laws, the suit challenges the legal adequacy of the city's Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) approved for a roughly 550-acre industrial area in Monticello Township earmarked for a potential large-scale technology and data center campus. Through this action, MCEA seeks a court order requiring the city to conduct additional, more rigorous environmental analysis, including a full Environmental Impact Statement (EIS), to accurately study and mitigate projected resource demands, which might include an estimated 250 to 300 million gallons of annual water usage and substantial electricity consumption. Both the city and the developer have denied the allegations and asked the court to dismiss the case, maintaining that the existing Monticello data center environmental review complies with state standards and that the claims are speculative. Because the matter remains open, there is no final outcome yet, following the close of discovery and the filing of summary judgment motions in October 2026.

shortName: In re Consumers Energy Co.
citation: In re Application of Consumers Energy Co. for Ex Parte Approval of Amendments to Rate GPD, No. U-21859 (Mich. Pub. Serv. Comm'n Nov. 6, 2025) (order).
summary: On February 7, 2025, Consumers Energy Company filed an application with the Michigan Public Service Commission seeking ex parte approval of amendments to its General Primary Demand Rate establishing a data center provision. The proceeding concerns Michigan public utility ratemaking and tariff regulation, administrative contested-case procedures, statutory clean-energy requirements, and the allocation of infrastructure costs associated with large electricity loads. The Data Center Coalition, business associations, the Michigan Attorney General, environmental and clean-energy organizations, and consumer advocates intervened, prompting the Commission to order a contested case on March 13, 2025. On November 6, 2025, the Commission approved amended service terms for data centers and other qualifying large-load customers, including minimum contract periods, billing requirements, collateral, and termination provisions intended to protect existing ratepayers from cost shifting. Following the Attorney General's December 8, 2025 petition for rehearing, the Commission denied rehearing on February 19, 2026, leaving the approved tariff provisions in place.

shortName: In re Griffin
citation: In re Griffin, No. 03-26-00652-CV, 2026 WL 3022768 (Tex. App. Oct. 8, 2026).
forum: "Third Court of Appeals at Austin, Texas"
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: On July 20, 2026, Pamela Griffin, Jose Orta, Carrie D'Anna, and Sarah Winters (collectively, "Relators") filed a petition for writ of mandamus in the Third Court of Appeals of Texas, against the City of Taylor and five officials in their official capacities. The Relators challenged the City Council's determination that the proposed ordinance prohibiting data centers in existing zoning districts could not be placed on the ballot, arguing that the City Charter imposed a ministerial duty to call an election and that the Council's private determination violated the Texas Open Meetings Act. The Relators sought a writ of mandamus directing the Taylor City Councilmembers to call an election on the petition for direct legislation and a determination that the City Council's non-public determination was void. On October 8, 2026, the Third Court of Appeals of Texas denied the petition for writ of mandamus.

shortName: Young v. Village of Commercial Point
citation: Young v. Village of Commercial Point, No. 2026CI0139 (Pickaway Cnty. Ct. Com. Pl. dismissed Sept. 30, 2026).
forum: Pickaway County Court of Common Pleas
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Taise Young, Jarrod Gibbon, and Bob and Sherri Fahringer, each a neighboring property owner, filed a complaint for declaratory and injunctive relief against the Village of Commercial Point, Ohio, K-Nova, LLC, K-Nova II, LLC, and Amazon Data Services, Inc. in the Pickaway County Court of Common Pleas on May 20, 2026. The plaintiffs challenged the validity of Village Ordinance 2024-07, which had rezoned approximately 267 acres from Exceptional Use to Planned Industrial District to accommodate a proposed data center development. They contended that the Village Council’s May 20, 2024 vote to dispense with the ordinance’s three required readings fell short of the three-fourths majority mandated by Ohio Revised Code § 731.17(A)(2), and that the ordinance’s emergency clause failed to satisfy the reason-stating requirement of Ohio Revised Code § 731.30. The plaintiffs sought a declaration that the ordinance was invalid and that the property’s zoning reverted to its pre-2024 classification, along with preliminary and permanent injunctive relief and costs. Amazon Data Services was voluntarily dismissed from the case without prejudice in June 2026, and the remaining defendants moved to dismiss on standing grounds before the court held depositions of each plaintiff. The plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed the entire action on September 30, 2026, and the case is now closed.

shortName: Minnesota Ctr. for Envir. Advocacy v. City of Lakeville
citation: Minn. Ctr. for Env't Advoc. v. City of Lakeville, No. 19HA-CV-25-5103 (Minn. Dist. Ct. dismissed May 26, 2026).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy filed a lawsuit against the City of North Mankato and Project Deacon, LLC to challenge how the city handled the environmental review for a major local project. The lawsuit invoked state environmental laws, arguing that the city failed to properly study and disclose the true plans for the development, a large-scale data center, thought to cause heavy strains on local water and energy resources. Ultimately, the case was resolved when the parties agreed to dismiss it, resulting in a closed status by April 2026.

shortName: Hazelnut LLC v. Town of Groton
citation: 327-449 Hazelnut LLC v. Town of Groton, No. KNL-CV-23-6064329-S, 2025 WL 2319439 (Conn. Super. Ct. Aug. 5, 2025).
category: Common Law: Torts
summary: On November 2, 2023, 327-449 Hazelnut, LLC filed a lawsuit in the Connecticut Superior Court, Judicial District of New London, against the Town of Groton. The plaintiff initially brought a negligence claim, alleging that the Town Council failed to act in a reasonably prudent manner when it voted to discontinue negotiations for a municipal fee agreement with data center developer NE Edge, a potential buyer of the plaintiff's property. The plaintiff later amended its complaint to substitute its negligence count and add a declaratory judgment count, alleging that the Town Council usurped the planning and zoning board's authority by determining the suitability of the plaintiff's property for data center development. The plaintiff sought more than $2 million in damages. On August 5, 2025, the court granted the defendant's motion to strike both the negligence and declaratory judgment counts. On August 25, 2025, the plaintiff withdrew the action against all defendants without costs to any party.

shortName: Lansdowne Conservancy v. SCC
citation: Lansdowne Conservancy v. State Corp. Comm'n, Nos. 250492–250495, slip op. (Va. Feb. 19, 2026).
summary: In 2024, Virginia Electric and Power Company sought Virginia State Corporation Commission approval of the Aspen-Golden and Apollo–Twin Creeks transmission projects in Loudoun County to address growing electricity demand and grid reliability needs associated with data centers. The proceedings involved Virginia transmission siting requirements under Va. Code § 56-46.1, including project necessity, environmental and historic impacts, local planning, and underground alternatives. Loudoun County and Lansdowne Conservancy opposed portions of the overhead routes, proposing instead to place approximately three miles of the Aspen-Golden line underground along Route 7. On February 5, 2025, the Commission approved both projects, rejecting the underground alternative over feasibility, cost, timing, and environmental-analysis concerns. The parties appealed, challenging the Commission's evaluation of project need, routing, underground feasibility, and mitigation measures; on February 19, 2026, the Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed the approvals in consolidated appeals Nos. 250492–250495.

shortName: Cologix COL5, LLC v. 655 Dearborn Park Lane, LLC
citation: Cologix COL5, LLC v. 655 Dearborn Park Lane, LLC, No. 24-3319 (6th Cir. Dec. 12, 2024).
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit vacated and remanded the district court’s grant of a motion for judgment on the plaintiff’s pleadings. Plaintiff Cologix purchased a 4-acre parcel of land from Defendant Dearborn (parcel owner). Cologix purchased the land parcel conditionally to be able to build a “data center facility” there. A provision allowed Plaintiff to terminate the contract if not satisfied that it could develop the land parcel as a data center facility. Contract also entitled Plaintiff to its downpayment being returned upon proper termination. Upon inspecting the property, Cologix found a natural gas pipeline & easement that potentially disrupted the property’s ability to be connected to nearby power lines. Plaintiff informed Defendant of intention to terminate the contract based on this fact. Defendant refused to return the down payment, and this is the point at issue for the Plaintiff. Court found that Cologix “must not be satisfied” that it could develop the property as a data center in order to terminate the lease. The Court found that  Cologix’s dissatisfaction “must be demonstrated to a degree that would satisfy a reasonable person”. The court found that Cologix must show that it was reasonably unsatisfied after conducting its due diligence land parcel analysis. The lower court's judgment was vacated, and the case was remanded, as the appellate court did not think that Cologix's dissatisfaction was reasonably based on its due diligence property analysis.

shortName: Berkeley Cnty. Council v. Government Properties Income Trust LLC
citation: Berkeley County Council v. Government Properties Income Trust, LLC, Nos. 20-1019, 20-1022 (W. Va. Nov. 10, 2022).
forum: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Government Properties Income Trust LLC owned a commercial building in Falling Waters, Berkeley County, West Virginia, that included a 30,875-square-foot computer room or data center, which the Berkeley County Assessor valued at $4,212,200 in fair market value and $2,527,320 in assessed value for the 2019 tax year. Government Properties appealed the assessment to the Berkeley County Board of Assessment Appeals, which affirmed the Assessor’s valuation, and Government Properties then appealed to the Circuit Court of Berkeley County, which reversed the Board and reduced the assessed value to $540,000 based on a fair market value of $900,000. Berkeley County Council, sitting as the Board, appealed to the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, arguing that the circuit court erred by proceeding without joining the Assessor as an indispensable party and by adopting the taxpayer’s appraisal over the Assessor’s cost-approach valuation. The appeal was consolidated with a related case, No. 20-1022, involving a similarly situated taxpayer referred to as Martinsburg IRS OC. In a decision issued November 10, 2022, the Supreme Court of Appeals reversed the circuit court in both cases and remanded with instructions to enter an order affirming the Board, holding that the taxpayers had not met their burden of showing the Assessor’s valuations were erroneous.

shortName: Stop the Hermantown Data Center v. City of Hermantown
citation: MCEA and Stop the Hermantown Data Center v. City of Hermantown and Harmony Group, LLC, No. 69DU-CV-25-3448 (St. Louis Co. Dist. Ct. filed Nov. 5, 2025)
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: On November 5, 2025, the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy (MCEA) and Stop the Hermantown Data Center (SHDC) challenged the City of Hermantown’s environmental study of the “Project Loon” data center proposal in St. Louis County District Court. Public records show that the City knew the project was for a data center approximately one year before it told the public its intended use. MCEA and SHDC claim that the City’s Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) was insufficient under the Minnesota Environmental Policy Act because the proposal does not describe the project’s intended use as a data center (it indicates the use is light industrial) and does not correctly describe the power or water usage of the project, nor does it discuss ways to mitigate potential impacts of the water or power use or air, light, and noise pollution on the surrounding community. They are seeking that the Court declare that the City must restart its environmental review process, enjoin the start of construction on the project, and enjoin the City from issuing any related permits. The City then announced that they would complete a new AUAR and MCEA, and SHDC agreed to pause the lawsuit until the new AUAR was completed. On October 5, 2026, the City unanimously approved the revised AUAR. An appeal can be filed until November 4, 2026, but none has been filed as of October 23, 2026.

shortName: Park View Estates Homeowners Association Inc. v. Kipper LLC
citation: Park View Ests. Homeowners Ass'n, Inc. v. Kipper LLC, No. CJ-2025-331 (Okla. Dist. Ct. Payne Cnty. filed Aug. 19, 2025).
category: Common Law: Property
summary: On August 19, 2025, Park View Estates Homeowner's Association, Inc. filed a lawsuit in the District Court of Payne County, Oklahoma, against Kipper, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of Google, Inc., Manhattan Construction Group, LLC, Olsson, Inc., and Emery Sapp & Sons, Inc. The plaintiff initially brought claims for public nuisance, private nuisance, and negligence, alleging that the defendants failed to implement adequate stormwater pollution prevention measures before beginning mass grading of the Google Data Center site, allowing red mud and silt to flow onto its property and substantially interfering with the use and enjoyment of its ponds, creeks, and surrounding private recreation areas. The plaintiff sought damages in an amount to be proven at trial, abatement and full restoration and remediation of its land to its former condition, temporary and permanent injunctions preventing further uncontrolled erosion and sediment runoff onto its property, and attorneys' fees and costs. On June 9, 2026, the plaintiff moved to substitute Manhattan-TW, a joint venture, for the incorrectly named Manhattan Construction Group, LLC. On August 3, 2026, the plaintiff filed an amended petition retaining the private nuisance claim, replacing the public nuisance and separate negligence counts with a trespass count, and requesting punitive damages. The case remains open, and no final decision appears in the available docket.

shortName: MCEA v. City of Hermantown
citation: Minn. Ctr. for Env’t Advocacy v. City of Hermantown, No. 69DU-CV-25-3448 (Minn. Dist. Ct. St. Louis Cnty. filed Nov. 5, 2025).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: In May 2025, the city announced it would conduct an environmental study called an Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) for an industrial project proposed by Harmony Group LLC. mentioned. On October 20, 2025, the city council approved rezoning of the neighborhood where the project is proposed. On November 5, 2025, the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy and Stop the Hermantown Data Center sued the City of Hermantown and Harmony Group LLC in St. Louis County District Court, asking the court to require proper environmental review and to stop construction and the issuance of permits until the review was complete. The plaintiffs alleged that the AUAR was not adequate because the city never disclosed that the project was a data center or did not do the proper due diligence to understand its environmental impacts. On December 9, 2025, the city rejected the lawsuit’s claims, saying an environmental review had already been completed. In March 2026, the city announced that Google was behind the project and that it would update the AUAR, and the plaintiffs agreed to put the lawsuit on hold while it did so. According to MCEA, Harmony Group indicated it would not move forward with the project while the new AUAR was underway. The case has since been reopened, and on October 21, 2026, the court issued an order reserving a motion.

shortName: Minnesota Ctr. for Envir. Advocacy v. City of Pine Island
citation: Minn. Ctr. for Env’t Advocacy v. City of Pine Island, No. 25-CV-25-2298 (Minn. Dist. Ct. Goodhue Cnty. filed Oct. 16, 2025).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: On October 16, 2025, the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy (MCEA) sued the City of Pine Island and Ryan Companies, US, Inc. in Goodhue County District Court. MCEA asked the court to reverse the city’s approval of the Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) for the Google-backed data center development about 482 acres north of Pine Island, because the AUAR was insufficient. MCEA argues that a more stringent Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) should be required. In May 2026, the court issued a temporary restraining order halting construction of the data center and denied the City’s and Ryan Companies’ request to rule that the AUAR complies with the law. On October 19, 2026, MCEA moved for summary judgment, and a hearing is scheduled for November 16, 2026.

shortName: GW Acquisition Co., LLC v. Pageland Limited Liability Co.
citation: GW Acquisition Co. v. Pageland Ltd. Liab. Co., No. 23-1611 (4th Cir. June 9, 2025) (unpublished), aff'g No. 1:22-cv-255, 2023 WL 125018 (ED. Va. Jan. 6, 2023).
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: On March 8, 2022, plaintiff GW Acquisition Co., LLC (a data center developer affiliated with QTS) filed the lawsuit against Pageland, LLC, Barbara Brower, and Jon Sanders Brower (sellers of land for development). The case was filed in the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, Alexandria Division. It's a diversity breach of contract action over a Purchase and Sale Agreement (PSA) for land in Prince William County for the Digital Gateway Project. The sellers brought third-party claims against broker Mary Ghadban and MagLandBroker, LLC. The court entered a declaratory judgment ordering Pageland LLC to "support and cooperate with" the plaintiff in obtaining approval of rezoning. It also found that Pageland, LLC breached the PSA, rejected the sellers' contract and tort claims, and later awarded the plaintiff's attorney's fees. The sellers appealed to the 4th Circuit. On June 9, 2025, after argument on May 7 2025, the Fourth Circuit affirmed in an unpublished opinion, calling the case "one of seller's remorse."

shortName: Applicants Mark and Joan Lippi, et al., Appeal, Tobyhanna Township Board of Supervisors' enactment of Ordinance No. 580
citation: Applicants Mark and Joan Lippi, et al., Appeal, Tobyhanna Township Board of Supervisors' enactment of Ordinance No. 580
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: On December 15, 2025, the Tobyhanna Board of Supervisors (Monroe County, PA) adopted Ordinance No. 580, which created a data center overlay district, defined data center use, and added data center use as a permitted use to the data center overlay district. Mark and Joan Lippi, Jennifer Beardsley, Dolores Ruppel, Jim Millington, the Stoddartsville Association and Ray Laytham appealed the decision, claiming that the Ordinance “creates unlawful spot zoning, contradicts the intended purpose of the Township’s rural residential district, and is for the specific and exclusive benefit of a single landowner, Pennsylvania Glacial Till, LLC." The petitioners are seeking that the Zoning Hearing Board invalidate the Ordinance. Public hearings have been held on March 11, 2026, and June 22, 2026. The next public hearing is scheduled for October 29, 2026.

shortName: Archbald I LLC v. Archbald Borough Council
citation: Archbald I LLC v. Archbald Borough Council, No. 2026-02773 (Pa. Ct. Comm. Pleas, filed Apr. 24, 2026)
forum: "Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas, Lackawanna County"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Archbald I, LLC filed a conditional use application with Archbald Borough County in Lackawanna County Court to build a data center campus on December 16, 2025 (“Project Scott”). The Council denied this application on March 27, 2026. Archbald I, LLC filed a land-use appeal against Archbald Borough County on April 24, 2026 claiming that the Council’s denial "violated the procedural requirements of the state Municipalities Planning Code, abused its discretion, erred as a matter of law and acted in bad faith." In August 2026, a judge allowed the Lackawanna County Housing Authority and resident Jack Swingle to join the case opposing the construction of the data centers. The case is still pending as of October 2026.

summary: Plaintiff zColo is a Delaware data center company. Zayo Group entered a lease with defendant Markley on March 21, 2014, and assigned the lease to plaintiff zColo September 24, 2020. Plaintiffs claim that Markley refuses to recognize zColo’s rightful position as tenant under the Lease. Plaintiff claims that landlord Markley engaged in a years-long harassing letter-writing campaign while demanding over seventy million dollars in connection with a Lease that requires standard annual rent payments starting at $63,708.00. Markley has refused to answer zColo’s request for necessary remediation work at the Property and refuses to recognize zColo’s right to extend the Lease per its terms. zColo wants the court to interpret the lease to settle the matter, and the plaintiff hopes to collect damages (as it considers the defendant’s behavior to be a breach of the lease). The plaintiff ultimately filed a notice of voluntary dismissal.
