summary: A data center developer appealed a county court ruling to the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania. The developer is seeking to quash a municipal ordinance that it claims was put in place after it submitted a development plan for a data center. The ordinance in this case was established by North Beaver Township.

shortName: Bockrath v. Coweta Cnty.
citation: Bockrath v. Coweta Cnty., No. [unavailable] (Ga. Super. Ct. Coweta Cnty. filed May 5, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Residents of Coweta County filed suit against Coweta County and Atlas Development, LLC in Coweta County Superior Court. The plaintiffs seek to void the rezoning of 829 acres from Rural Conservation to Industrial zoning. The suit arises out of a proposed $17B, 13-building data center campus proposed by Atlas Development in December 2024. The Board of Commissioners approved the rezoning on April 7, 2026. The suit calls for a declaratory judgment and asks for judicial review of Coweta County's rezoning approval process. The plaintiffs include adjacent property owners Paula and Ronald Bockrath, Harvey Shelnut Jr., Quillian and Lillian Barber, Brian Beck, Robert Lytten, and other Coweta County residents opposing the development, including Steve Swope, one of the organizers of Citizens for a Rural Coweta. The lawsuit argues that the land is within an area designated as “Rural Places and Complete Communities" in Coweta County’s Comprehensive Plan and should not be used for industrial development. The media reports that the case also asks for a waiver of the county's sovereign immunity. The lawsuit alleges procedural violations and argues that the county disregarded groundwater recharge areas, wetlands, and watershed impacts, and calls for a new regional impact review.

shortName: In re Iris Energy Ltd. Securities Litigation
citation: In re Iris Energy Ltd. Sec. Litig., No. 1:24-cv-07046 (E.D.N.Y. dismissed Mar. 19, 2025).
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Securities
summary: Paul Williams-Israel filed suit against Iris Energy Limited, Belinda Nucifora, Daniel Roberts, and William Roberts in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York. Plaintiff, on his own behalf and representing other shareholders in the same situation, filed a class action complaint for violations of federal securities laws and seeks to recover losses and damages on behalf of the investors. The plaintiff alleges that the defendant, Iris Energy made false claims and omitted information regarding its data center and high-performing computing capabilities. As a result, investors suffered losses due to a decline in stock prices. On March 14, 2025, the lead plaintiff, Rick Bunney, filed a notice of voluntary dismissal, and on March 19, 2025, the case was dismissed without prejudice.

summary: West Virginia Citizen Action Group is initiating an administrative proceeding to challenge the state Department of Environmental Protection's issuance of a construction permit to MGS CNP1, LLC. The permit would allow MGS CNP1, LLC to build a wood-fired waste power plant in Mason County, West Virginia. The appellant alleges violations of the West Virginia Air Pollution Control Act and its implementation plan. In June 2026, MGS CNP1, LLC is reported to have abandoned its permit.

shortName: Nat’l Ass’n for Advancement of Colored People-Chesterfield Branch v. State Corp. Comm’n
citation: Nat’l Ass’n for Advancement of Colored People-Chesterfield Branch v. State Corp. Comm’n, No. 260476 (Va. filed May 27, 2026).
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The NAACP Chesterfield Branch appeals to the Supreme Court of Virginia from the State Corporation Commission proceeding, Case No. PUR-2025-00037. There, the State Corporation Commission approved the Dominion Energy’s Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center, a gas power plant. The appeal alleges violations of the Virginia State Air Pollution Control Law, the Virginia Administrative Process Act, the Virginia Environmental Justice Act, and the federal Clean Air Act.

summary: Interstate Power and Light (Alliant Energy) sought a certificate of public convenience from the Iowa Utilities Commission for a 720 MW gas plant called the Morgan Valley Energy Center. The plant is intended to meet demand from data centers, among other loads. Several objections have been loged in the docket based on transparency, air quality and siting concerns.

citation: Hairston Clan, Inc. v. Stokes Cnty., No. 26CV000198-840 (N.C. Super. Ct. filed Mar. 12, 2026).

summary: The National Hairston Clan, local families, and advocacy groups filed a lawsuit against the Stokes County Board of Commissioners, challenging their decision to rezone approximately 1845 acres of rural and agricultural land for an AI data center complex called "Project Delta." Plaintiffs request that the court reverse the rezoning actions due to a lack of procedural safeguards, factual analysis, and reasoned decision-making. The case is ongoing.

shortName: Independent Market Monitor for PJM v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
citation: Independent Market Monitor for PJM v. FERC, 162 F.4th 1167 (D.C. Cir. 2025)
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: On November 25, 2025, the Independent Market Monitor for PJM (IMM) filed a complaint against PJM with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”), which FERC reviewed and dismissed. IMM is now seeking a review of FERC’s decision by the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. After PJM excluded IMM from attending meetings between PJM’s Board of Managers and the Liaison Committee, IMM filed a complaint with FERC arguing that PJM’s action violated Section IV.G of its tariff. The Liaison Committee is a nonvoting body designed to facilitate communication between PJM Members and the Board. IMM attended these meetings for years before its exclusion. The court found that IMM lacked standing to challenge its exclusion because IMM failed to demonstrate a concrete or particularized injury resulting from its exclusion from Liaison Committee meetings. The court dismissed IMM’s petition for lack of jurisdiction due to IMM’s lack of standing.

shortName: Clean Air Coalition of Western New York, Inc. v. New York State Public Service Comm'n
citation: Clean Air Coal. of W. N.Y., Inc. v. New York State Pub. Serv. Comm'n, 249 AD3d 1446 (N.Y. App. Div. 2026).
forum: "State of New York, Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Third Judicial Department"
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: Clean Air Coalition of Western New York challenged the New York Public Service Commission’s ruling allowing Digihost to acquire a natural-gas-fired generating facility for a cryptocurrency-mining operation. The plaintiff alleged that the Public Service Commission violated the Climate Leadership and Protection Act by failing to consider the impact on disadvantaged communities or to interfere with the attainment of the greenhouse gas emissions limits. In May 2026, the Third Department affirmed the Supreme Court's finding that the Public Service Commission's approval did not satisfy its statutory obligation.

shortName: In re Duke Energy Progress, LLC
citation: In re Duke Energy Progress, LLC & Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, 2026 Solar Resource Procurement Request for Proposals, Nos. E-7, Sub 1356 & E-2, Sub 1406  (N.C. Utils. Comm’n filed Mar. 9, 2026). AND In re Duke Energy Progress, LLC & Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, 2026 Solar Resource Procurement Request for Proposals, No. 2026-56-E (S.C. Pub. Serv. Comm’n 2026).
summary: On March 17, 2026, Duke Energy Progress, LLC and Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC filed information concerning their proposed 2026 solar and solar-plus-storage procurement before the North Carolina Utilities Commission. The proceedings invoke state public utility law, integrated resource planning, renewable energy procurement, and regulatory oversight of utility resource acquisition. The Commission issued an order on April 23, 2026, directing Duke Energy to defer its proposed solicitation pending a decision in a separate resource-planning proceeding. Industry and clean-energy advocacy organizations, including the Carolinas Clean Energy Business Association, Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, Sierra Club, and Vote Solar, challenged the deferral through requests for reconsideration. Duke Energy subsequently announced that it would not proceed with the 2026 solicitation and anticipated resuming procurement in 2027. As of October 1, 2026, the solicitation remained halted, with no verified final order formally closing both dockets.

shortName: Amazon Data Services Inc. v. Bd. of Supervisors of King George City
citation: Amazon Data Servs., Inc. v. Bd. of Supervisors of King George Cnty., No. CL25000315-00 (Va. Cir. Ct. filed Apr. 24, 2025).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Amazon Data Services ("ADS") filed a lawsuit against the King George County Board of Supervisors, appealing a March 2024 decision by the county Board of Zoning Appeals ("BZA"). The BZA denied the company's request for a determination of vested rights to construct a data center campus on 869 acres across nine parcels that ADS purchased for $168 million in 2023. In September 2023, the King George County Board of Supervisors originally approved rezoning the land for a massive data center campus, but a newly elected board majority later sought to pull out of the agreement. The parties reached mutual settlement in September 2026; King George County acknowledged ADS's vested rights to develop, and ADS agreed not to build data center structures along the Rappahannock River in addition to pledging $10 million toward the construction of a new Career and Technical Education building for King George Public Schools.

shortName: Haley v. X.AI Corp.
citation: Haley v. X.AI Corp.
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Jason Haley, Preston Herrington, and Taylor Logsdon filed a putative class-action lawsuit — on behalf of a class potentially including more than 10,000 residents of Southaven and Horn Lake, Mississippi — against X.AI Corp., SpaceX, and subsidiary MZX Tech, alleging that gas-fired turbines powering xAI's "Colossus" AI data center campus (which grew from roughly 3 to 57 turbines in under a year) create a public and private nuisance through near-constant roaring, humming, and low-frequency vibrations audible and felt in nearby homes 24 hours a day. Plaintiffs assert claims for private nuisance, public nuisance, negligence, negligence per se, and negligent infliction of emotional distress, and seek damages for loss of use and enjoyment of property, diminished property values, and emotional distress, as well as injunctive relief requiring the defendants to abate the noise.

shortName: Jokubas v. CloudBrothers
citation: Jokubas v. CloudBrothers, No. [docket number] (Sør-Rogaland tingrett filed Oct. 16, 2026) (Nor.).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities, Employment and Lobbying: Employment
summary: On October 16, 2026, a former data center engineer filed a lawsuit in Sør-Rogaland District Court, Norway, against Nscale and CloudBrothers. The plaintiff brought claims under Norwegian employment law, alleging that he worked at Nscale's Stavanger-area data center through CloudBrothers under an unlawful subcontracting arrangement and that Nscale acted as his employer by directing his daily work and shifts. The plaintiff further alleged that CloudBrothers dismissed him in retaliation after he objected to a warning that two weeks of holiday pay would be withheld for late vacation requests and raised concerns with Norway's Labor Inspection Authority. The plaintiff sought monetary compensation and a declaration that he was an Nscale employee.

shortName: BCB Cheyenne LLC v. MineOne Wyoming Data Center LLC
citation: BCB Cheyenne LLC v. MineOne Wyo. Data Ctr. LLC, No. 1:23-cv-00079 (D. Wyo. filed May 3, 2023).
forum: United States District Court for the District of Wyoming
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: Plaintiff wanted to build the largest Bitcoin mine in the US. To do so, it would need constant, inexpensive electrical power. Plaintiff selected a site in WY for the project, put land parcels under contract, identified resources, and worked to secure financing for the project. Plaintiff entered a contract with MineOne Wyoming Data Center to support the project, where MineOne would own the developments and finance them, and Plaintiff would implement and operate them. The two agreed that payment would come after the project's initial implementation phase was complete. Despite all of Plaintiff’s work/performance, Defendant sent a team and began to encroach on Plaintiff’s ability to perform duties. Defendant told Plaintiff that it sought to take control and replace the Plaintiff as operators of the site. Plaintiff (BCB Cheyenne) filed a complaint against Defendants (MineOne Wyoming Datacenter & partners) for breach of contract, anticipatory repudiation of contract, intentional interference with contractual relations, alter ego liability, enterprise liability, and lost profits and money damages. The judge granted a motion for voluntary dismissal of the case, and there was termination of procedures without judicial action (Oct 16, 2024), with each party to pay its own fees.

shortName: Gendreau v. McEvoy
citation: Gendreau v. McEvoy, 116 Va. Cir. 212 (2025).
docket: CL25-2187; appeal docketed as Record No. 2157-25-3 (Va. Ct. App.)
forum: "Circuit Court of the City of Roanoke, Virginia"
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: October 9, 2025, Henri Gendreau filed a petition for a writ of mandamus in the Circuit Court of the City of Roanoke against Mike McEvoy, Executive Director of the Western Virginia Water Authority (WVWA), alleging that WVWA violated the Virginia Freedom of Information Act by redacting water supply capacity figures tied to a proposed Google-affiliated data center in Botetourt County. WVWA asserted that the withheld information was exempt as proprietary information voluntarily provided by a private business under Va. Code § 2.2-3705.6(3). On November 5, 2025, the court granted Gendreau’s petition, finding that WVWA had not shown by a preponderance of the evidence that the information was proprietary, and ordered the records released. McEvoy entered an appeal to the Court of Appeals of Virginia on December 12, 2025 (Record No. 2157-25-3) and sought a stay of the circuit court’s judgment, which the Court of Appeals denied on January 28, 2026. As of the most recent docket entries, briefing was complete and the appeal remained pending with no disposition issued.

shortName: Rizzo v. Verizon CCC LLC
citation: Rizzo v. Verizon CCC LLC, No. 142489 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. Jan. 14, 2011) or Rizzo v. Verizon CCC LLC, 2011 N.Y. Slip Op. 50505(U) (Sup. Ct. Jan. 14, 2011).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Petitioner Mary Ann Rizzo challenged approvals granted for a Verizon project in the Town of Somerset under CPLR Article 78 and the State Environmental Quality Review Act. She argued that local agencies improperly approved the project without requiring a full environmental impact statement. The court rejected her claims and dismissed the petition.

shortName: State ex rel. Michael Isreal v. Maryellen O'Shaughnessy
citation: State ex rel. Isreal v. O'Shaughnessy, 2020-Ohio-3292 (Ohio Ct. App.)
forum: "Court of Appeals of Ohio, Tenth Appellate District"
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: In 2019, the pro se litigant Michael Isreal filed a mandamus action against Maryellen O'Shaughnessy, the Franklin County Clerk of Courts. The case was filed as an original action in the Court of Appeals of Ohio (10th Appellate District). Isreal wanted records showing when the clerk's e-filing system was down in 2018. The clerk submitted an affidavit from its Director of Information Technology, and the court found that the Data Center official who issued the report is not part of the clerk's office (where Isreal had requested the records). On Jun. 11, 2020, the court ruled on Isreal's objections to the magistrate's decision. The case was closed.

shortName: Lingelbach v. Twiggs Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs
citation: Lingelbach v. Twiggs Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs, No. [unavailable] (Ga. Super. Ct. Twiggs Cnty. Feb. __, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: At issue is a rezoning of land in Georgia. The Georgia Department of Community Affairs unanimously approved the rezoning in September 2025, and residents filed suit in Twiggs County Superior Court approximately a week later. The lawsuit (filed in Twiggs County Superior Court on September 25, 2025) alleges that Twiggs County ignored its own rules around zoning and public notices when the commission unanimously voted to rezone about 300 acres of agricultural land for a data center project. Weyerhaeuser Company, which owns millions of acres of timberland across the U.S., owns the property. The Twiggs County Local Code and Land Development Ordinance requires that a sign be posted on any property under consideration for rezoning at least 15 days in advance. The lawsuit alleges that Twiggs County placed the sign incorrectly, on the wrong property, and misstated the hearing date. The date was allegedly amended, but the sign was not placed on the correct piece of land until 9 days before the hearing date.

shortName: Dubose v. Cnty. of Imperial
citation: Dubose v. County of Imperial, No. ECU004709 (Cal. Super. Ct. Imperial Cnty. June 30, 2026).
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: On April 30, 2026, five Imperial County residents, Tom Dubose, Kevin Smith, Ryan Dickerson, Daryl Dickerson, and Carl Stills, represented by attorney Sebastian Rucci, the developer of the proposed data center, brought a suit in Imperial County Superior Court against the Imperial County Registrar of Voters to block a proposed data center ban measure, the Imperial County Data Center Prohibition Act, before it reached the November ballot. The petitioners claimed that the measure violates California’s single-subject rule for ballot initiatives and that it does much more than just ban large data centers, reaching into daily administrative tasks. The petitioners also challenged the measure’s enforcement provisions, its limits on future amendments, and its retroactivity clause going back to April 2. The case was dismissed on June 30, 2026.

shortName: In re Application of Ohio Power Co.
citation: In re Application of Ohio Power Co. for New Tariffs Related to Data Centers & Mobile Data Centers, No. 2025-1458 (Ohio filed Nov. 3, 2025) (appeal from Pub. Utils. Comm'n of Ohio No. 24-508-EL-ATA).
corporateEntities: AEP, Stargate manufacturing and data center site in Lordstown, OH  (Softbank, Oracle, OpenAI partnership), The Ohio Manufacturers' Association Energy Group, Ohio Power Co.,
summary: On November 3, 2025, the Ohio Manufacturers’ Association Energy Group filed an appeal with the Supreme Court of Ohio challenging the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio’s (PUCO) approval of Ohio Power Company, American Electric Power’s (AEP), data center tariff. The Ohio Manufacturers’ Association wants Ohio’s Supreme Court to reverse the decision allowing AEP to charge data centers differently than it does other power customers. The appeal concerns ratemaking and tariff regulations, statutory judicial review, and constitutional equal protection. The appellant, Ohio Manufacturers’ Association, contends that the approved tariff unlawfully discriminates against data center customers and fails to satisfy applicable ratemaking requirements, seeking reversal of the PUCO’s order made on July 9, 2025. The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel and AEP defend the PUCO's decision, maintaining that the tariff appropriately allocates infrastructure costs to large-load customers. PUCO denied applications for rehearing on September 3, 2025. Oral argument originally scheduled for August 6, 2026, was cancelled and rescheduled for an unknown later date. As of October 19, 2026, no final decision on the appeal or any additional information has been publicized.

shortName: Matter of Sierra Club v City of N. Tonawanda
citation: Matter of Sierra Club v. City of N. Tonawanda, 217 A.D.3d 1418 (N.Y. App. Div. 2023).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: The Sierra Club, along with individual petitioners Darlene Bullsover, Sylviu Dan, Jr., and Deborah Gondek, initiated a proceeding against the City of North Tonawanda, the Planning Board, Fortistar North Tonawanda LLC, and Digihost International, Inc., invoking New York Civil Practice Law and Rules (CPLR) Article 78. The petitioners sought to challenge the site plan approval for a Bitcoin mining facility and requested a preliminary injunction to halt the project. The New York State Supreme Court denied the motion for a preliminary injunction and granted the respondents' motions to dismiss the Article 78 petition with prejudice.

shortName: Solar Energy Industries Association v. FERC
citation: Solar Energy Indus. Ass’n. v. FERC, 154 F. 4th 863 (D.C. Cir. 2025).
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: On May 27, 2021 Solar Energy Industries Association, a utility, filed a petition for review of a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) order certifying the Broadview solar power facility in Montana as a “small power production facility” under the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (“PURPA”) in the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. FERC previously defended its interpretation as reasonable and within its expertise, and the D.C. Circuit affirmed under Chevron. Petitioners then petitioned for cert to the Supreme Court of the United States. SCOTUS granted cert, vacated the D.C. Circuit court’s judgment, and remanded for further consideration in light of Loper Bright. On September 9, 2025 the D.C. Circuit applied the statute without deference under Loper and again upheld FERC’s decision certifying Broadview solar power facility as a “small power production facility.”

shortName: Bluemile, Inc. v. Atlas Industrial Contractors, Ltd.
citation: Bluemile, Inc. v. Atlas Industrial Contractors, Ltd., 12 CV 5597, 12 CV 5768 (Ohio Ct. Com. Pl. Feb 25, 2014)
forum: "Court of Appeals of Ohio, Tenth Appellate District"
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: Plaintiff Bluemile provides cloud/data services via its Columbus, OH data center. Defendant Atlas Industrial Contractors had a technician on site who used a non-insulated screwdriver and caused an electrical short circuit, disrupting data provision services by Plaintiff for two hours. Plaintiff suffered loss of income. Plaintiff sought insurance coverage from its insurance provider (Hartford) and was owed insurance compensation following court proceedings with their insurance company. Plaintiff formally appraised the value of the lost income during the 2-hour stretch: $718,202—$545,282 in cell services and $172,920 in cloud/data provision income. Bluemile and Hartford sued the Defendant for breach of duty/negligence and to recover insurance damages, respectively. Atlas reached a settlement with Hartford for $315k before trial. The Court held Atlas accountable financially and said that it was liable for 1 million in voice/cell damages and was allowed a setoff of 315k (amount settled with Hartford) to avoid paying more than 100% of the damages Atlas proximately caused.

shortName: Riera Graterol v. Allison-Smith Co. LLC
citation: Riera Graterol v. Allison-Smith Co., No. 25EV009856 (Ga. State Ct. Fulton Cnty. filed Sep. 22, 2025).
category: Common Law: Torts
summary: On September 22, 2025, Perpetio Antonio Riera Graterol and Noris Maritza Azuaje Montilla, as surviving parents of Anthony J. Riera Azuaje, and Hillary B. Cranford, as representative of his estate, filed a lawsuit in the State Court of Fulton County, Georgia, against Allison-Smith Company LLC. The case is classified as a general tort action. The plaintiffs allege that the defendant's negligent installation of temporary electrical equipment during construction of a data center caused Anthony J. Riera Azuaje's injuries and death, and that the defendant acted in bad faith and failed to follow applicable electrical safety standards. The plaintiffs seek damages for Azuaje's conscious pain and suffering, funeral and burial expenses, lost wages and earning capacity, and the full value of his life, as well as punitive damages. The case remains open, and no final decision appears in the available docket.

shortName: Burke v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty.
citation: Burke v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty., No. CL24000334-00 (Va. Cir. Ct. filed Jan. 12, 2024), rev'd in part, No. 2025-24-4 (Va. Ct. App. Mar. 31, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: A group of Gainesville-area residents filed suit against the Board of Supervisors of Prince William County in December 2023. The residents sought to block the construction of the PW Digital Gateway, which was expected to become the largest data center corridor in the world. Plaintiffs alleged that it was illegal for the Board of County Supervisors to grant approval of 23 million square feet of data centers on roughly 2100 acres. The circuit court sustained the Board's demurrer and dismissed the landowner's challenges with prejudice. Plaintiffs filed an appeal that was jointly heard with Oak Valley Homeowners Association, Inc., et al. v. Prince William County Board of County Supervisors, et al., and the court held that the circuit court erred in sustaining the Board's demurrer to the landowners' claims and found that the county's public hearing advertisements were legally insufficient for notifying the public about the Digital Gateway data center project before approving the rezoning.

shortName: Masaitis v. Coreweave, Inc.
citation: Masaitis v. CoreWeave, Inc., No. 2:26-cv-00355 (D.N.J. filed Jan. 12, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the District of New Jersey
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Lobbying
summary: Raymond Masaitis filed suit against CoreWeave, Inc., Michael Intrator, Nitin Agrawal, and Brannin McBee in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey. The plaintiff, individually and representing other investors in the same situation, filed a class action complaint for violations of federal securities laws, seeking to recover losses and damages. The investors represented are the ones who purchased or acquired CoreWeave securities between March 28, 2025, and December 15, 2025. The plaintiff alleges that defendants committed fraud when they provided false information and omitted material facts regarding the defendant CoreWeave's capability to satisfy customer demand and rely on one supplier. When the problems became public, investors suffered losses due to a decline in the stock price.

shortName: Havron v. City of Bessemer
citation: Havron v. City of Bessemer, No. 68-CV-2025-000025.00 (Ala. Cir. Ct., dismissed June 22, 2026).
corporateEntities: Logistics Land Investment, LLC; Hyperscale "Project Marvel"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: A group of local residents filed suit against the City of Bessemer, Alabama, in 2025, alleging that the city didn't provide proper public notice about rezoning 700 acres of timberland slated for a $14 billion data center development called "Project Marvel." The case was dismissed in June 2026 after the residents and the city jointly agreed to drop the case and allow the construction of the campus to proceed.

shortName: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC v. United City of Yorkville
citation: Preserve Our Yorkville & Cmty., LLC v. United City of Yorkville, No. 2026CH10 (Ill. Cir. Ct. 2026).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Preserve Our Yorkville (a group of residents of a local farm) initiated a suit in the Kendall County Chancery Court against the City of Yorkville, invoking civil equitable laws and local zoning ordinances. The plaintiffs argue that the city improperly prioritized private development over the public benefit, and seek equitable remedies to block the construction of Project Steel and Project Cardinal, which are 1,000-plus-acre data center developments that residents claim would introduce constant construction and replace agricultural land with industrial operations within feet of their homes. While there is no final judicial decision, a bench trial remains scheduled for April 26 and 27, 2027; reports indicate that the city and the plaintiffs are close to reaching a settlement.

shortName: NSI 6, LLC v. Benton County, Missouri, et al.
citation: NSI 6, LLC v. Benton Cnty., No. 26BE-CC00056 (Mo. Cir. Ct., Benton Cnty. filed Aug. 24, 2026)
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Benton County passed an Order and Ordinance for a temporary ban (6 months, with a possible additional 6 month extension) on data centers for the purposes of due diligence on August 10, 2026. NSI 6, LLC, owns property in Benton County that it plans to use to construct a data center. On August 24, 2026, NSI 6, LLC sued Benton County and Commissioners Steve Daleske, Scott Harms and Larry Berry in Benton County Circuit Court. NSI 6 claimed that the ordinance was a zoning or land-use enactment that the County did not have the authority to adopt under Missouri zoning enabling acts. NSI 6 seeks declaratory judgment that the County did not have the authority to enact the ordinance and that ordinance is void, invalid, and unenforceable as well as injunctive relief prohibiting the County and the Commissioners from implementing the ordinance. On October 6, a preliminary injunction prohibiting, restraining and enjoining the Defendants from enforcing, applying, implementing or threatening to enforce the order was ordered until a final judgment is reached. The case is still pending as of November 2026.

shortName: Valtrus v. Lumen
citation: Valtrus Innovations Ltd. v. Lumen Technologies, Inc., No. 1:26-cv-03928 (N.D. Ill. Apr. 8, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois
category: Corporate: IP

shortName: Seidel v. Atlas Power Holdings (ND), LLC
citation: Seidel v. Atlas Power Holdings (ND), LLC, No. 53-2023-CV-01519 (N.D. Dist. Ct. Williams Cnty. filed Oct. 12, 2023).
category: Common Law: Property
summary: On October 12, 2023, Corey Seidel and twenty-one other residents filed a lawsuit in the District Court of Williams County, Northwest Judicial District, North Dakota, against Atlas Power Holdings (ND), LLC, and Williams County. The plaintiffs brought claims for private nuisance, public nuisance, and trespass, alleging that noise and vibrations from the Atlas Power Data Center entered their properties, harmed their quality of life and health, and reduced their property values, and that Williams County failed to enforce its zoning ordinances and improperly re-zoned the property to heavy-industrial use. The plaintiffs sought at least $50,000 in damages from Atlas Power over claims of nuisance and trespass, injunctive relief requiring Atlas Power to reduce the noise or permanently cease operations, and an order requiring Williams County to enforce its zoning ordinances against Atlas Power and reverse the allegedly improper zoning change. On September 16, 2024, the court dismissed the trespass claim and the claims against Williams County, while allowing the remaining claims against Atlas Power to proceed. On June 12, 2025, a notification of settlement was filed. On March 13, 2026, the court issued an order to stay litigation proceedings. The case remains open, and no final decision appears in the available docket.

shortName: Pearson v. Port of Morrow
citation: Pearson v. Port of Morrow, No. 2:24-cv-00362-SI (D. Or. filed Feb. 28, 2024).
forum: United States District Court for the District of Oregon
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: A group of Oregon residents brought a putative class action in the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon against the Port of Morrow and several other defendants, alleging that defendants' disposal of wastewater caused contamination in groundwater. They assert a claim under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, and common law claims under Oregon state law. In a separate but related action, several of the same plaintiffs sued Amazon Data Services over alleged contributions to the same nitrate-contamination problem: Pearson v. Amazon Data Servs., Inc., No. 2:26-cv-00633-SI (D. Or. filed Mar. 31, 2026); that action is proceeding through a proposed class settlement.

shortName: No Desert Data Center v. Pima Cnty.
citation: No Desert Data Ctr. Coal. v. Pima Cnty., No. C20260314 (Ariz. Super. Ct. dismissed Apr. 13, 2026).
forum: Superior Court of Arizona in Pima County
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: The No Desert Data Center Coalition filed suit against Pima County and its Planning and Zoning comission over the approval of a data center complex planned for a roughly 290 acre site ("Project Blue"). Plaintiffs alleged that Pima County officials violated Arizona's Open Meeting Law and did not disclose the purpose of rezoning in its agenda. A Pima County Superior Court judge dismissed the suit, ruling PIma County did not violate the Open Meeting Law. The Coalition has announced plans to file an appeal while construction on Projecct Blue has moved forward.

shortName: Owens-Pearson v. City of Memphis
citation: Owens-Pearson v. City of Memphis, No. 2:26-cv-03358-TLP-tmp (W.D. Tenn. Oct. 20, 2026).
category: Other
summary: Six Memphis residents sued the City in the Western District of Tennessee, alleging that restrictions on public comments and bans from council meetings violated their First Amendment rights and constitutional equal protection guarantees. The plaintiffs seek to invalidate the council's speech and decorum restrictions and prevent enforcement of meeting-attendance bans imposed following protests over a proposed data center moratorium. On October 20, 2026, the court partially granted a temporary restraining order, prohibiting enforcement of the plaintiffs' attendance bans and certain speech restrictions.

shortName: Mack Paramus Co. v. Mayor & Council of Borough of Paramus
citation:
Mack Paramus Co. v. Mayor & Council of Paramus, 511 A.2d 1179 (N.J. 1986).
(New Jersey court documents: 103 N.J. 564, 511 A.2d 1179 (1986).)
forum: "Superior Court of New Jersey, Law Division, Bergen County"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Plaintiffs in this case are Mack Paramus Co. and affiliated Mack partnerships and corporations. Plaitiffs challenged the Borough of Paramus' Sunday closing ordinance in an action in lieu of prerogative writs. Intervenor Excelsior Panbro Companies, Inc. brought a parallel challenge to Midland Park's ordinance. The Law division invalidated the ordinances as preempted by state law, and the Appellate Division affirmed. In July 1986, the Supreme Court of New Jersey held that the legislature's adoption L. 1979, c. 178 did not preempt or supersede local Sunday closing regulations. On remand, the Law division addressed the Plaintiffs' constitutional challenges. The case is closed.

shortName: Residents Miles Crosby and Jennifer Singleton filed a lawsuit against Colleton County in January 2026, challenging county zoning changes that allowed data centers in rural portions of the county via a special-exception process. The parties reached a settlement in October 2026 that prohibits data center development across much of the Ashepoo, Combahee, and Edisto (ACE) Rivers Basin and requires the County to establish a "Data Center Exclusion Area."
citation: Crosby v. Colleton Cnty., No. 2026-CP-15-00021 (S.C. C.P. Colleton Cnty. filed Jan. 9, 2026).
forum: Colleton County Court of Common Pleas
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Colleton County, South Carolina residents Miles Crosby and Jennifer Singleton, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, sued Colleton County to challenge a newly passed zoning ordinance allowing data centers to be built in rural areas of the county via a "special exception" permit. Plaintiffs allege the ordinance violates South Carolina zoning law, the county's own comprehensive plan, and its zoning code; the suit was filed shortly after developer Eagle Rock Partners applied under the new ordinance to build an 859-acre, 1,000-megawatt data center complex — potentially one of the largest in the country — within the ACE Basin, a 1.7-million-acre, largely undeveloped watershed around the Ashepoo, Combahee, and Edisto rivers. Plaintiffs argue the project would harm the area's rural character, dark night skies, water quality, and wildlife, and ask the court to invalidate the ordinance.

shortName: Newsom v. Amazon Data Services, Inc.
citation: Newsom v. Amazon Data Servs., Inc., No. 3:25-cv-00074, 2026 WL 1993954 (W.D. Va. July 10, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia
category: Common Law: Property
summary: On August 11, 2025, Austin W. Newsom and Central VA Marine filed a lawsuit in the Circuit Court for Louisa County, Virginia, against Amazon Data Services, Inc. On September 15, 2025, the defendant removed the action to the United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia. The plaintiffs brought claims for private nuisance and temporary injunctive relief, alleging that construction of the defendant's Northeast Creek Technology Campus interfered with their use and enjoyment of the property, caused structural damage to Newsom’s house, and led Central VA Marine customers to refrain from seeking boat services at the property. The plaintiffs sought an order temporarily enjoining the defendant from further construction on the Amazon property. The plaintiffs sought at least $1 million in damages plus interest and an order temporarily enjoining the defendant from further construction on the Amazon property. On May 6, 2026, the plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction barring unreasonable interference with their use and enjoyment of the property, rather than halting construction entirely. On July 10, 2026, the court granted in part and denied in part the defendant's motion to dismiss, allowing the private nuisance claim to proceed while dismissing the standalone claim for temporary injunctive relief because an injunction is a remedy rather than an independent cause of action. The case remains open, and no final decision appears in the available docket.

shortName: Application of Entergy Texas, Inc. to Amend Its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity
citation: Application of Entergy Texas, Inc. to Amend Its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity, Docket No. 56693 (Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex. June 3, 2024).

shortName: Caruthers v. Sangamon Cnty.
citation: Caruthers v. Sangamon County, No. 2026MR000236 (Ill. Cir. Ct. Sangamon Cnty. filed July 6, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Several residents sued Sangamon County and its County Board on July 6, 2026, seeking to overturn the county's approval of the CyrusOne data center. The lawsuit challenges the county's April 7 approval of a conditional permitted use for a 280-acre agricultural site to build a data center. The plaintiffs include members of the Caruthers family. The suit claims the April 7th resolution is misdated and relies on an Illinois law that treats county zoning decisions as legislative decisions subject to fresh judicial review. The plaintiffs ask the court to declare the approval invalid. They argue that the project fails the ordinance's mandatory standards, that the board's findings have no rational basis, that placing an industrial use in the agricultural district is arbitrary, and that the petition was incomplete. They also argue that the county's July 2025 data center ordinance conflicts with the comprehensive plan. The case is ongoing.

shortName: Stines et al v. PrimeBlock Operations, LLC et al
citation: Stines et al v. PrimeBlock Operations, LLC et al
forum: United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina
category: Common Law: Property
summary: Murphy, North Carolina residents Judith Stines and William Huffman filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against California-based Bitcoin-mining company PrimeBlock, its affiliate Exponential Digital LLC (formerly Ankr Mining Solutions), and contractor Innotech Z Inc., alleging that a cryptocurrency-mining and AI data center operating since mid-2021 emits unrelenting noise from its servers, generators, and cooling systems — reaching as high as 90 decibels — that has "shattered" the rural community's quality of life and diminished property values for an estimated 1,000 property owners within a two-mile radius. Plaintiffs assert claims for private and public nuisance, negligence, gross negligence, and willful or wanton conduct, alleging the operators have refused to invest in basic noise-abatement measures such as soundproof barriers or vibration-dampening equipment, and seek both compensatory and punitive damages on behalf of the proposed class.

shortName: State ex rel. Mayes v. Arizona Corp. Comm'n
citation: State ex rel. Mayes v. Ariz. Corp. Comm’n, No. CV2026-007458 (Ariz. Super. Ct., Maricopa Cnty. filed Feb. 18, 2026).
forum: Superior Court of Arizona in Maricopa County
summary: On February 18, 2026, the State of Arizona, via Attorney General Kristin K. Mayes, filed a complaint in the Superior Court of the State of Arizona in and for the county of Maricopa concerning the Arizona Corporation Commission’s approval of an energy supply agreement between Tucson Electric Power and a customer associated with the Project Blue data center. The matter invokes Article 15, § 3 of the Arizona Constitution, judicial review under A.R.S. § 40-254(A), and declaratory-judgment law under A.R.S. § 12-1831 et seq. The State of Arizona contends that the Commission unlawfully adjudicated both its exclusive ratemaking authority and its constitutional duty to ensure reasonable and just rates by allowing unregulated side agreements with customers, thereby impacting rate schedules. Intervenor, Tucson Electric Company, filed a motion to dismiss. The State of Arizona petitioned the court to expedite consideration, declare the agreement unlawful, vacate the commission’s decision, and remand with instructions. As of October 1, 2026, the case is currently “under advisement ruling”, with no final decision issued.

shortName: Tonawanda Seneca Nation v. Genesee Cnty. Industrial Development Agency
citation: Tonawanda Seneca Nation v. Genesee Cnty. Indus. Dev. Agency, No. E72421 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. filed July 1, 2025).
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: In July 2025, the Tonawanda Seneca Nation and the Sierra Club initiated a Special Proceeding in the Genesee County Supreme Court against the Genesee County Industrial Development Agency (doing business as the Genesee County Economic Development Center, or GCEDC), Stream U.S. Data Centers LLC, and the Town of Alabama. Invoking New York Civil Practice Law and Rules (CPLR) Article 78 and the State Environmental Quality Review Act (SEQRA), the petitioners alleged that the GCEDC violated both procedural and substantive environmental review mandates, as well as the Final Generic Environmental Impact Statement (FGEIS) for the site, by relying on conceptual plans rather than actual specifications and failing to coordinate its review with the Town of Alabama's site plan review. Through the lawsuit, the petitioners sought a Temporary Restraining Order to halt development and aimed to invalidate two March 2025 GCEDC resolutions that concluded the environmental review and awarded $472 million in tax subsidies for a proposed 900,000-square-foot data center at the Western New York Science and Technology Advanced Manufacturing Park (STAMP), located adjacent to the Tonawanda Seneca Nation Reservation and the Iroquois National Wildlife Refuge. The proceeding ultimately concluded with the case being disposed of after the GCEDC Board of Directors voluntarily rescinded its consistency determination and final resolution in September 2025. Following the retraction of these approvals, the Tonawanda Seneca Nation and the Sierra Club filed to dismiss the litigation without prejudice in October 2025, securing their objective of vacating the initial approvals while Stream U.S. Data Centers and the GCEDC pivoted toward evaluating an expanded, multi-billion-dollar project application subject to a new review under SEQRA and General Municipal Law.

citation: City of Sulphur Springs v. Luminant Mining Co., LLC, No. 06-26-00025-CV, 2026 WL 2107168 (Tex. App. July 22, 2026).

In its original petition, the plaintiff brought claims for declaratory judgment, fraudulent concealment, common-law fraud, civil conspiracy, and, alternatively, quiet title. The plaintiff sought to challenge a deed restriction prohibiting commercial electricity production, generation, or storage on property it sought to develop for a data center with an on-site power plant. The plaintiff sought a declaration that the covenant was void and unenforceable, actual and exemplary damages, pre-judgment and post-judgment interest, attorneys' fees, and court costs. On appeal, the plaintiff argued that Vistra failed to establish a probable right to recovery and that the district court's temporary injunction order failed to comply with Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 683. summary: Mack Paramus Co., Mack Paramus Affiliates, Mack Development Company and Mack Paramus Parkway Co., Mack Development Corp. and Mack Office Park, Inc., filed a prerogative writs action against the Mayor and Council of the Borough of Paramus in the Supreme Court of New Jersey. The plaintiffs sought declaratory relief to permit the operation of computers in commercial offices on Sundays, arguing that it is an essential activity. The court denied the relief regarding the unconstitutional allegations and upheld the ordinance, but ruled in part that the activity in question is essential and, therefore, may be carried out on Sundays.

summary: Colin Doyle, Friends of the Irish Environment CLG, Futureproof Clare, Martin Knox, and Christine Sharp sought judicial review of two planning permissions granted by An Bord Pleanála (Ireland's national planning appeals board) in April 2024 for a large data center and substation development near Ennis, County Clare — comprising six two-story data halls (over 118,000 square meters) powered partly by 66 diesel generators and a 120MW gas facility, plus a new 110kV substation. summary: Gregory Paul Guido Jr., a Harlem, Georgia resident, filed petitions for judicial review challenging the Columbia County Board of Commissioners' February 2026 approvals rezoning the White Oak Business Center and Pumpkin Center properties to Data Center District zoning for two large data center campuses. Guido alleges the county approved the rezonings without a verified water-usage or sewer-capacity analysis required by the county's Water and Sewer Division, relied on a stale traffic study prepared for an earlier version of the White Oak project, and failed to analyze the impacts of shifting the project's primary access point. citation: Beaver Ventures LLC v. Washington County Assessor, TC-MD 240646N, 2026 WL 221842, at *1 (Or. Tax M. Div. Jan. 27, 2026).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Beaver Ventures LLC, which owns the PDX 11 and PDX 12 data center facilities in the Hillsboro enterprise zone, appealed the Washington County Assessor’s denial of an enterprise zone (EZ) property tax exemption to the Oregon Tax Court, Magistrate Division, on December 9, 2024. Plaintiff held two separate EZ authorizations, a 2017 authorization covering the initial construction phase (PDX 11) and a 2023 authorization covering a later phase (PDX 12), but in April 2024 it filed only a single combined EZ claim form and property schedule rather than separate claims corresponding to each authorization, as required by Oregon Administrative Rule 123-674-3500(3). On September 9, 2024, the Assessor denied the exemption for the 2023 investments in PDX 12 and assessed approximately $3.4 million in additional property taxes. Plaintiff argued that its single filing substantially complied with the statutory claim requirements and that neither the City of Hillsboro, the enterprise zone sponsor, nor the Assessor adequately communicated that a second claim form was necessary. Following cross motions for summary judgment and oral argument held September 16, 2025, the court granted summary judgment to the Assessor on January 27, 2026, holding that the substantial compliance doctrine does not apply to enterprise zone exemption claims and that Plaintiff’s failure to timely file a separate claim could not be cured on appeal. The decision is unpublished, and the 60-day window to appeal to the Regular Division has since passed with no indication of further appeal.

summary: This is a Commission-initiated regulatory investigation rather than adversarial litigation. shortName: Coresite, LLC v. Cnty. of Fairfax
citation: CoreSite, LLC v. County of Fairfax, Record No. 0510-25-4 (Va. Ct. App. June 16, 2026).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: CoreSite, LLC, a data center company that leases space in four Reston, Virginia facilities to roughly 300 customers, challenged the County of Fairfax’s authority to compel disclosure of its customers’ names after the County summoned CoreSite in January 2024 under Virginia Code § 58.1-3110 to identify customers potentially liable for personal property taxes on equipment stored at the data centers. CoreSite filed a petition for declaratory judgment and a motion to quash the summons in the Circuit Court of Fairfax County, arguing that the County lacked statutory authority to investigate customers of unknown tax status, that the County had not “specifically identified” any taxpayers as the statute requires, and that a confidentiality provision in CoreSite’s customer agreements barred disclosure absent a court order. The circuit court granted summary judgment to the County on all three grounds, and CoreSite appealed. In a published opinion issued June 16, 2026, the Court of Appeals of Virginia held that Virginia Code § 58.1-3109(6) gives the County broad authority to investigate the tax status of data center customers, but that the County’s January 2024 summons failed to comply with Code § 58.1-3110’s requirement to “specifically identify” taxpayers, and that the confidentiality provision’s carveout for governmental requests did not bar disclosure in any event. The Court of Appeals affirmed the circuit court’s judgment in part, reversed it in part, and remanded the case with instructions to vacate the order enforcing the January 2024 summons, without prejudice to the County issuing a new, compliant summons.
