summary: A group of non-profits and tribes sued federal officials challenging an approval of an R-line which is a 226-mile, 345 KW, $835M electric transmission line running throughout Nebraska. The United States Fish and Wildlife Service granted Nebraska Public Power District (“NPPD”) “emergency” approval to construct the R-Line without consulting affected tribes relying on Executive Order 14156, which declared a national energy emergency and invoked emergency provisions under the National Historic Preservation Act. The federal district held for project’s opponents on 8 June 2026 and held that federal officials likely violated federal because opponents will lose their legally protected procedural interest if construction proceeds as planned.

shortName: Valtrus v. Digital Realty
citation: Valtrus Innovations Ltd. v. Digital Realty Trust, Inc., No. 2:24-cv-00535 (E.D. Tex. July 12, 2024).
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas
category: Corporate: IP

shortName: Protect Sand Springs Alliance, Inc. v. City of Sand Springs
citation: Protect Sand Springs Alliance, Inc. v. City of Sand Springs, No. CV-2026-439 (Tulsa Cnty. Dist. Ct., filed Mar. 5, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Plaintiffs are challenging a zoning decision by the City of Sand Springs who challenged the standing of plaintiffs. The court ultimately dismissed all claims without prejudice.
secondaryCategory: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Procedural, Public Meeting, and Notice Requirements

shortName: In re Frederick Cnty. Data Center Referendum Committee
citation: In re Frederick Cnty. Data Ctr. Referendum Comm., No. 67, Sept. Term 2025 (Md. July 24, 2026).
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: In September 2025, the county council voted on Bill 25-09, which set the rules for creating a data center zone and limited data center development to an initial 1% of the county, and in December 2025, the county council approved Ordinance 26.01.001, establishing a 2,600-acre data center zone north of Adamstown. A group of data center developers and landowners sued the Frederick County Data Center Referendum Committee in Frederick County Circuit Court over the committee’s petition for a referendum, which opposed how large the data center zone was on the map the county council had approved. The issue in the trial court was whether the ordinance is a law subject to referendum according to the county charter, and whether the committee followed the correct procedure for the petition. On June 18, 2026, the court ruled that the ordinance is not subject to referendum and that the petition forms were inadequate because the overlay maps they used to collect signatures were not printed in color, making them indistinguishable. The Frederick County Data Center Referendum Committee appealed to the Supreme Court of Maryland, and in a per curiam order on June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court affirmed the lower court’s judgment. As a result, the referendum on the data center overlay map cannot be placed on the November ballot.

shortName: ECO TIP West, LLC v. Chatham Cnty.
citation: ECO TIP West, LLC v. Chatham Cnty., North Carolina, 26CV000456-180 (Chatham Cty. Superior Ct., filed April 23, 2026)
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions

shortName: Foxglove v. Secretary of State for Housing, Communities & Local Government
citation: Foxglove; Global Action Plan planning appeal under s. 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990
category: Other

shortName: GW Acquisition Co., LLC v. Pageland Limited Liability Co.
citation: GW Acquisition Co. v. Pageland Ltd. Liab. Co., No. 23-1611 (4th Cir. June 6, 2023).
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: Plaintiff Mary Ann Ghadban (real estate broker) was hired by Jon Brower (son of Barbara Brower) (Defendants) to help sell 131 acres of land in VA. Ghadban worked for Plaintiff GW Acquisition Co. (real estate developer attempting to obtain the 131 acres for data center construction). Court found that Defendants breached contractual obligations to assist GWA in obtaining the County’s approval for the parcel’s rezone. Defendants did not assist but rather impeded rezoning processes by not signing the necessary documents on time (and only signed the necessary rezoning documents under court order). Defendants said they were unhappy with the price paid for the land. The court sided with the development company and said that the Defendant’s behavior was seller’s remorse and not fair behavior.

shortName: Silver Fox 606 LLC vs. Village of Indiantown
citation: Silver Fox 606 LLC v. Village of Indiantown, No. 26001122CAAXMX (Fla. Cir. Ct. Martin Cnty. filed Oct. 7, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Procedural, Public Meeting, and Notice Requirements
summary: Silver Fox 606 LLC, a data center company, sued Indiantown Planning, Zoning and Appeals Board, challenging the Board's decision to hear a resident's appeal of an administratively approved property plat for its Project Silver Fox data center. Silver Fox alleges violations of Florida land use and zoning laws. On October 13, 2026, the court granted an injunction blocking the scheduled October 19 appeal hearing and directed the Village to explain why the hearing should proceed.
secondaryCategory: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions

shortName: Vill. of Monroeville v. Gray Matter Advisors, Inc.
citation: Vill. of Monroeville v. Gray Matter Advisors, Inc., 2026-Ohio-2110 (2026)
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: The appeals court affirmed the trial court's appointment of a receiver due to insolvency based on defaults on payments to creditors and conversion of corporate property, among other issues. The suit originally arose from breach of an energy services agreement by the appellant who operated a data center. The respondent filed for claims of breach of contract, fraud, fraudulent transfer, and asserting alter ego liability. The trial court appointed an emergency receiver to protect against imminent insolvency.

shortName: FLX Strong v. Town of Lansing Zoning Bd. of Appeals
citation: In re FLX Strong v. Town of Lansing Zoning Bd. of Appeals, 2026 N.Y. Slip Op. 76311(U) (N.Y. App. Div. 3d Dep’t Sept. 8, 2026)
forum: "State of New York, Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Third Judicial Department"
corporateEntities: TeraWulf, Inc., Lake Hawkeye, LLC; Cuyahoga Operating Co., LLC
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary:
The Appellate Court denied a motion to appeal a decision by a lower court. The decision sought for appeal was a claim brought by FLX Strong and CLEAN., two grassroots organization seeking to challenge the decision by the Lansing Town Zoning Board that the former site of a power plant classified for Industrial/Research use could be repurposed for a data center. The previous ruling is entered as an exhibit in the appeal filings.

In the previous ruling, the Zoning Board (and the developers) sought to dismiss the claim on the basis that the plaintiffs (FLX Strong et al.) lacked standing to bring a suit in the matter of the data center zoning, and that the case was not ripe because future zoning decisions could ameliorate their concerns. The lower court ruled that the plaintiffs did have standing because the organization members could have their enjoyment of the surrounding nature disturbed and may experience noise impacts. It ruled that the case was ripe and that the plaintiffs stated a claim for relief, because they challenged the Zoning Board’s decision which permitted the project to proceed. 

The lower court denied the motion to dismiss the claim, and the Appellate Court denied the subsequent appeal. There have been no further updates on this case as of October 22nd, although the Lansing Town and the State of New York are considering bans on data center development.

shortName: King Sykes LLC v. City of Chicago
citation: King Sykes LLC v. City of Chicago, No. 23-CV-1636, 2024 WL 730375 (N.D. Ill. Feb. 22, 2024).
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois
category: Constitutional Law: Takings
summary: On March 15, 2023, King Sykes, LLC filed a lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, against the City of Chicago, three City officials in their official capacities, Scott Goodman, GRIT Chicago, LLC, and Farpoint Development, LLC. The plaintiff initially brought federal civil rights claims for a taking without just compensation, denial of class-of-one equal protection, and conspiracy, and a state-law claim for tortious interference with prospective economic opportunity, alleging that the defendants conspired to scare off potential buyers and make the plaintiff's property unmarketable so that the City and Goodman could later purchase it at a discount. The plaintiff sought judgment in its favor on the takings claim, damages and compensation for the value of the property allegedly taken by the City, compensatory and punitive damages estimated to exceed $15 million on each of Counts II–IV, and reasonable attorneys' fees, costs, and expenses. On July 20, 2023, the plaintiff filed an amended complaint omitting two of the three City officials as defendants. On February 22, 2024, the court dismissed the amended complaint without prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction to the extent the federal claims were not ripe and for failure to state a claim to the extent the federal claims were ripe, declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state-law claims, and granted the plaintiff leave to file a second amended complaint by March 29, 2024. The plaintiff did not file a second amended complaint by the deadline. On April 24, 2024, the court closed the case.

shortName: Nordhoff-Net LLC v. Comm'r
citation: Nordhoff-Net LLC v. Commissioner, No. 1750-26 (T.C. petition filed Mar. 10, 2026).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Nordhoff-Net LLC petitioned the U.S. Tax Court to redetermine a roughly $24 million tax deficiency the IRS assessed against the partnership, arguing that its acquisition of data centers and its improvements to a previously damaged building should not have triggered the additional tax liability the Commissioner determined was owed.

shortName: Scranton v. Ransom
citation: Scranton v. Ransom, No. 2026-01296 (Lackawanna Cnty. Ct. Com. Pl. filed Mar. 02, 2026)
forum: "Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas, Lackawanna County"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Scranton Materials is suing the Ransom Township Board of Supervisors in the Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas, Lackawanna County, claiming that the Ransom Township Zoning Ordinance unlawfully omits data centers as a use under the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code. Scranton owns a parcel of land in Lackawanna County. In November 2025, Scranton filed a substantive validity challenge and proposed amendments to the Ransom Township Zoning Ordinance to include a data center overlay zoning district to cover their parcel of land. The Board of Supervisors granted a motion for non-suit at the day of the hearing. Scranton seeks that the Court declare that the Ordinance excludes data centers and that their proposed amendments should be accepted so that they can build a data center on the land. The case is pending as of October 2026.

shortName: Caparoula v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty.
citation: Caparoula v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty., No. 1137-24-4 (Va. Cnty. Ct. 2024), aff’d, 2025 WL 2649495, No. 1042-25-3 (Va. Ct. App. 2025)
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: William Caparoula and other neighbors (“Neighbors”) filed suit against the Board of County Supervisors of Prince William County and Stanley Martin Holmes, LLC (“Stanley”) in Prince William County Circuit Court on December 23, 2023. Stanley owned a parcel of land that they wanted to rezone from Planned Mixed Residential to M-2 (light industrial). The Board held three public hearings and the majority of the citizens that attended were opposed to the rezoning. The Board approved the rezoning. The neighbors claimed that the Board’s approval of the Ordinance was “arbitrary and capricious” and sought to overturn the Board’s approval. The Board and Stanley filed demurrers and the case was dismissed on June 6, 2024. On July 8, 2024, the neighbors appealed and on September 16, 2025, the appellate court affirmed.

shortName: No Desert Data Center v. Pima Cnty.
citation: No Desert Data Center v. Pima Cty., No. 2 CA-CV 2026-0180 (Ariz. Ct. App., filed May 11, 2026 ).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: The No Desert Data Center Coalition, a local community organization, seeks an Order to Show Cause and invalidate a Pima County zoning decision regarding Project Blue under Arizona's open meetings law. Project Blue is an under-construction Beale Infrastructure sponsored hyperscale data center project with two phases requiring approximately 300 MW of electricity per phase. The county court dismissed the case and the plaintiffs filed an appeal with the Arizona Court of Appeals, Division 2, in May 2026, which is pending as of October 2026.

shortName: Sierra Pacific Power Co. v. Tract (Landco.) I
citation: Sierra Pac. Power Co. v. Tract (Landco) I, LP, No. CV26-02142 (Nev. Dist. Ct. argued Sept. 29, 2026).
forum: "Washoe County, Nevada Second Judicial District Court		"
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: Sierra Pacific Power Company BDA ("NV Energy") filed suit against Tract ("LANDCO") I LP and Reno Power NR 1 LLC in the Washoe County Second Judicial District Court of the State of Nevada on July 24, 2026. The plaintiff filed a complaint seeking a declaration that the Demand filed by the defendants related to electricity supply, service obligations, and rates cannot be included as an arbitration clause and remain within the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada's authority. Plaintiff seeks a declaration that Defendant Tract cannot pursue arbitration against NV Energy. The plaintiff also seeks injunctive relief to stop the arbitration in the subjects related to the petition until Commissions' 2026 is concluded.

shortName: Blackboard Inc. v. International Business Machines Corp.
citation: Blackboard Inc. v. Int'l Bus. Machs. Corp., No. 1:21-cv-07165 (S.D.N.Y. June 2, 2022).
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of New York
category: Arbitration
summary: Blackboard Inc. filed a petition against International Business Machines Corporation (IBM) in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Under the Federal Arbitration Act, the petitioner sought to annul the Award from May 27, 2021, or, alternatively, to reduce it and avoid the accrual of interest. The award discussed was related to a Master Professional Services Agreement signed between the parties and stipulated that the petitioner had to pay $29,793.24 for incorrectly withheld payments and a second counterclaim. The court denied the petition to annul or modify and confirmed the award from the arbitration case because petitioner failed to demonstrate enough reasons to justify a decision to vacate or modifiy the award. The court agreed with the third relief related to pre-decision interest.

shortName: Haas v. Goochland Cnty.
citation: Haas v. Bd. of Supervisors of Goochland Cnty., No. CL25001270-00 (Goochland Cnty. Cir. Ct. filed Dec. 4, 2025).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Cynthia Haas, Peggy Knisley, Virginia H. Reed, and Gail A. Minnick, each a resident and property owner in Goochland County, Virginia, filed suit against the Goochland County Board of Supervisors, the County Planning Commission, and Goochland County in the Circuit Court for the County of Goochland, challenging the Board’s November 6, 2025 adoption of a Technology Overlay District ordinance that expanded permitted data center, generator, and energy-storage uses across more than one hundred parcels, including land previously zoned for agricultural use. The plaintiffs allege that the County failed to satisfy the advertisement, notice, and public hearing requirements of Virginia Code sections 15.2-1433, 15.2-2204, and 15.2-2285, and that the ordinance applies inconsistent standards to similarly situated parcels in violation of the uniformity requirement of Virginia Code section 15.2-2282. They further contend that provisions governing backup generators and mandatory connection to public water and sewer systems exceed the County’s authority under the Dillon Rule and conflict with state statutes, and that several of the ordinance’s standards are unconstitutionally vague. The plaintiffs seek a declaration that the ordinance is void ab initio, an injunction barring its enforcement, and an order requiring the County to follow proper notice and hearing procedures before any future rezoning. The case remains pending as of the date of the complaint.

shortName: Kyndryl, Inc. v. Computer Sciences Corporation et al
citation: Kyndryl, Inc. v. Comput. Scis. Corp., 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 197405 (2026)
forum: United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts
category: Corporate: Arbitration
summary:
Plaintiff Kyndryl, Inc. subcontracted with defendant Computer Sciences
Corporation (“CSC”), a subsidiary of defendant DXC Technology Company. Kyndryl was to provide data storage services to an end user under this contract. The Master Services Agreement (“MSA”) contract granted CSC exclusive rights over certain services. Under the MSA, Kyndryl tried to “descope” certain services. The complaint at issue alleges that under the MSA, descoping is a valid termination mechanism of the contract. The complaint alleges that the defendants are in material breach of their contract. The litigant's cross-motions to dismiss were granted in part and denied in part.

shortName: Coll v. Hollenback Twp. Bd. of Supervisors
citation: Coll v. Hollenback Twp. Bd. of Supervisors, No. 202603611 (Luzerne Cnty. Ct. Com. Pl. filed Mar. 24, 2026)
forum: "Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas, Luzerne County"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Over thirty landowners in Hollenback Township proposed a curative amendment to the Hollenback Township Zoning Ordinance to rezone 460 acres of rural land from agricultural-residential to industrial so that data centers could be built on the land. The Hollenback Township board of supervisors denied this request on procedural grounds. On March 24, 2026, Craig Coll and approximately thirty additional landowners filed an appeal from a zoning board hearing. This case is pending as of October 2026.

shortName: Ohio Environmental Council v. State
citation: Ohio Env’t Council v. State, No. 25CV009387 (Ohio Ct. Com. Pl. Franklin Cnty. filed Oct. 24, 2025).
forum: Franklin County Court of Common Pleas
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The Ohio Environmental Council sued the State of Ohio, challenging air pollution law amendments passed as a part of the state budget passed in 2025. The plaintiffs allege violations of the One Subject Rule of the Ohio State Constitution, which mandates that every bill must contain only one subject, clearly expressed in its title. They allege that the air pollution amendments, which would limit civil nuisance enforcement and prohibit the Ohio EPA from using community air monitoring data, bear no relationship to the state budget. The presiding judge issued a ruling on October 16, 2026, declaring the amendments unconstitutional.

shortName: In re Wisconsin Power & Light Co.
citation: In re Application of Wis. Power & Light Co. for Approval of an Individual Contract Rate Service Agreement for a Large Load Customer in Beaver Dam, Wis., No. 6680-TE-115 (Wis. Pub. Serv. Comm'n May 2026) (decision).
corporateEntities: Meta, Alliant Energy, Wisconsin Power & Light
summary: On April 29, 2025, Wisconsin Power and Light Company applied to the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin for approval of an individual contract rate agreement to serve a proposed 220-megawatt data center in Beaver Dam owned by Meta subsidiary Degas, LLC. The proceeding concerns utility rate regulation under Wis. Stat. § 196.192, including whether the agreement adequately protects other customers from increased rates and costs attributed to the data center. The Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, Clean Wisconsin, and Wisconsin Industrial Energy Group intervened, raising concerns regarding cost allocation, financial guarantees, termination charges, contract duration, and transparency. Following additional disclosure requirements in February 2026, the Commission approved the agreement with modifications on May 7, 2026, strengthening financial safeguards, reporting requirements, and protections against cost shifting while requiring a separate large-load tariff for future customers. The Commission issued its final written decision on June 18, 2026, approving the agreement subject to conditions.

shortName: Henrico 183 LLC v. DeKalb County
citation: Henrico 183 LLC v. DeKalb County , No. 26CV7218 (Ga. Super. Ct. DeKalb Cnty. Aug. 5, 2026)
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: Dekalb County is being sued by a data center developer over its temporary moratorium for data center permits. The developer claims they received assurances of approval from the county. Originially the project was proposed as a film studio in 2022. The County claims a moratorium is not a final decision and the plaintiffs missed a 12-month deadline to file their claims.

shortName: City of Hilliard v. Logue
citation: City of Hilliard v. Logue, ERAC Case No. 25-7227 (Ohio Env’t Rev. Appeals Comm’n filed Nov. 7, 2025), appeal withdrawn Sept. 15, 2026.
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The City of Hilliard filed the administrative appeal with the Ohio Environmental Review Appeals Commission, challenging the issuance of a permit for AEP Ohio's Hilliard Fuel Cell Facility at the proposed Amazon Web Services data-center site. The appeal alleges that the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency failed to give notice to the City prior to the issuance of the permit. In September 2026, the City withdrew its appeal.

shortName: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
citation: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin, 575 S.W.3d 92 (Tex. Ap.–Houston [14th Dist.] 2019), aff'd in part, rev'd in part, 620 S.W.3d 692 (Tex. 2021).
forum: Court of Appeals for the Fourteenth District of Texas
category: Constitutional Law: Takings
summary:
Data Foundry (Plaintiff) operated data centers in Austin, TX, and purchased its electricity from Austin Energy (the sole entity that provides electricity in that municipality and is owned by the City of Austin (Defendant)). Austin Energy proposed a new rate structure; Data Foundry challenged this in administrative hearings, and then sued in court on the basis that the proposed rates were discriminatory and excessive. The city filed a motion to dismiss the case on the basis of Texas Rule 91a (i.e., the claim had no basis in law or fact). The trial court dismissed the case on the basis of Data Foundry lacking standing.
On appeal, the appellate court ruled that Data Foundry had standing because it was being required to pay higher charges, but the court ruled that rate review was not within the jurisdiction of the courts.
On appeal to the Texas Supreme Court, the court ruled that Data Foundry had standing and ordered that the trial court rule on jurisdiction and whether the rates proposed were discriminatory.

shortName: State ex rel. K-Nova II, LLC v. Village of Commercial Point
citation: State ex rel. K-Nova II, LLC v. Vill. of Com. Point., No. 2026-0694 (Ohio filed June 3, 2026)
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: The State of Ohio ex rel. K-Nova II, LLC is suing the Village of Commercial Point, its administrators, and its council members in the Supreme Court of Ohio. K-Nova owns two parcels that are currently zoned for single use as data centers. They submitted an application to begin the building-permit process for a data center on this land on April 1, 2026. On May 4, 2026, the village passed an 18-month moratorium on data center construction. The relators are seeking a peremptory writ of mandamus for their application to be processed under the Site Plan Review Process that was in effect under city ordinances at the time they submitted their application. The case is pending as of October 2026.

shortName: Paulus v. Citicorp North America, Inc.
citation: Paulus v. Citicorp N. Am., Inc., No. 2:12-CV-00856, 2014 WL 4557603 (S.D. Ohio Sept. 12, 2014).
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio
category: Common Law: Property
summary: On August 3, 2012, Kurt W. Paulus and Janene Paulus filed a lawsuit in the Delaware County Court of Common Pleas, Ohio, against Citicorp North America, Inc. and Citigroup Technology, Inc. On September 18, 2012, the defendants removed the action to the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. The plaintiffs brought claims pursuant to Ohio common law for negligence and recklessness, public nuisance, and private nuisance, alleging that noise from power generators used at the defendants' data center disturbed them and interfered with their use and enjoyment of their property. The plaintiffs sought compensatory and/or special damages, punitive damages, and an injunction requiring the defendants to abate the loud noise from the data center generators, pre-judgment interest, expert witness fees, costs, and attorney fees. On September 12, 2014, the court denied the plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment and granted in part and denied in part the defendants' motion for summary judgment, dismissing the public nuisance claims while allowing the absolute and qualified private nuisance claims to proceed and treating negligence and qualified private nuisance as one cause of action. On March 9, 2015, the parties filed a stipulation of dismissal with prejudice consistent with their Settlement and Release Agreement.

shortName: In re Virginia Electric & Power Co.
citation: In re Application of Va. Elec. & Power Co. for Approval & Certification of Golden-Mars Transmission Facilities, No. PUR-2025-00056 (Va. State Corp. Comm'n Apr. 9, 2026) (order).
summary: On March 28, 2025, Virginia Electric and Power Company, doing business as Dominion Energy Virginia, applied to the Virginia State Corporation Commission for approval of the Golden-Mars high-voltage transmission project in Loudoun County to address increasing electricity demand associated with regional data center development. The proceeding concerns Virginia transmission siting and certificate-of-public-convenience-and-necessity requirements under Va. Code §§ 56-46.1 and 56-265.2, including grid reliability, environmental impacts, routing alternatives, and underground construction. Local homeowners' associations, community organizations, and school authorities opposed aspects of the proposed overhead routes, citing concerns about proximity to residences and schools. On April 9, 2026, the Commission authorized the project, identified Route 4 as its preferred alignment, conditionally designated Route 3A as an alternative, and found underground construction infeasible. Following the Loudoun County School Board's refusal to consent to Route 4, the Commission issued a final order on June 29, 2026, approving Route 3A and dismissing the proceeding. Homeowners' associations and the School Board subsequently petitioned for reconsideration, and on July 20, 2026, the Commission declined to suspend its final order while those challenges were considered.

shortName: Valenzuela v. Alliance Cloud Services, LLC
citation: Valenzuela v. All. Cloud Servs., LLC, No. 1:26-cv-01694 (W.D. Mich. filed May 26, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan
category: Common Law: Property
summary: On May 26, 2026, Lindy Valenzuela and John Valdes, on behalf of themselves and all others similarly situated, filed a proposed class-action lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan against Alliance Cloud Services, LLC, which owns and operates the data center located at 415 E Prairie Ronde Street, Dowagiac, Michigan 49047-1348 ("Data Center"). In their original complaint, the plaintiffs brought claims for private nuisance, public nuisance, and negligence, alleging that the Data Center emitted unreasonable and excessive noise that substantially interfered with their use and enjoyment of their properties and reduced their property values. The plaintiffs sought class certification, designation as class representatives and appointment of their counsel as class counsel, judgment in their favor, compensatory and exemplary damages, pre-judgment and post-judgment interest, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief not inconsistent with the defendant's local, state, and federal regulatory obligations. On August 13, 2026, the court dismissed the defendant's motion to dismiss as moot after the plaintiffs filed an amended complaint. The case remains open, and no final decision appears in the available docket.

shortName: Intergate Quincy II LLC v. Grant Cnty.
citation: Intergate Quincy II LLC v. Grant County, No. 232001807 (Wash. Super. Ct., Douglas Cnty., filed June 2, 2023).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Intergate Quincy II LLC and Intergate Quincy LLC, data center operators owned by Sabey Data Centers, filed suit against Grant County, Washington, in Douglas County Superior Court on June 2, 2023, challenging the Grant County Assessor’s valuation of their Quincy data center facility for the 2020 and 2021 tax years. According to media coverage, the Assessor valued the property at approximately $239 million for 2020 and $237 million for 2021, while Plaintiffs contend the correct values were approximately $132 million and $123 million, respectively. Plaintiffs state they paid roughly $3.3 million in property taxes under protest over the two tax years and seek a refund of approximately $2 million they allege was based on the excess valuation. The case was assigned to Douglas County Superior Court rather than Grant County Superior Court because Grant County is a named defendant. A similar valuation dispute was previously brought against Grant County by H5 Data Centers in 2019. No docket entries or media coverage confirming the case’s current status beyond the June 2023 filing were located as of October 2026.

shortName: McDavid v. Scioto Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs
citation: McDavid v. Scioto Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs, No. 26CIH00167 (Scioto Cnty. Ct. Com. Pl. filed Feb. 18, 2026).
forum: Scioto County Court of Common Pleas
corporateEntities: Project Dazzler; Tilted Gate, LLC; Google
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: On February 18, 2026, Patrick McDavid filed suit in the Scioto County Court of Common Pleas against the Scioto County Board of County Commissioners and Commissioners Scottie Powell, Merit Smith, and Steven Mault, alleging violations of Ohio’s Open Meetings Act. The dispute arises from a Community Reinvestment Area tax agreement that the Board adopted in connection with a proposed Google data center project referred to as “Project Dazzler,” located in Franklin Furnace, Ohio. According to McDavid, the Board negotiated and discussed the terms of this agreement in executive session rather than during a public meeting, as the statute requires. Neither the docket entries nor the available media coverage specify what relief McDavid is seeking. The defendants answered the complaint on March 30, 2026; the matter appears to remain pending as of October 2026, and the trial is currently scheduled for April 2027.

shortName: Exoticridge Crypto Co., LLC v. Hawkins County Tennessee
citation: ExoticRidge Crypto Company LLC v. Hawkins County, Tennessee, 2:26-cv-00064, (E.D. Tenn., filed March 31, 2026)
forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee
category: Constitutional Law: Due Process
secondaryCategory: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions

shortName: Sharp v. City of Wilmington
citation: Sharp v. City of Wilmington, No. 1:26-cv-00448 (S.D. Ohio filed May 5, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio
category: Constitutional Law: Due Process
summary: Jessica and Logan Sharp filed suit against the City of Wilmington, its City Council and Planning Commission, Shirley Orwick, and Austin Powell in state court. The case was later removed to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. Twelve Wilmington residents have joined the case since its start, and Amazon Data Services, Inc. was included as an intervenor defendant. The plaintiffs sought to invalidate three approved ordinances that allow the development of an Amazon data center in the City of Wilmington. The plaintiffs claim that the defendants violated due process rights and failed to take enough measures to inform the residents about the ordinances. The defendants denied the accusations and argued that the laws were legally approved and that delaying the project would interfere with the economic development and health and safety aspects of the city. No final decision has been issued yet.

shortName: Eagan Capital, LLC v. City of Eagan
citation: Eagan Cap., LLC v. City of Eagan, No. 19HA-CV-26-3029 (Minn. Dist. Ct. Dakota Cnty. filed June 15, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Eagan Capital, which owns a data center in Eagan, sued the city on June 15, 2026. It asks the court to void the city's one-year moratorium on new or expanded data centers. The moratorium bars new data centers within 500 feet of homes or using more than 20 megawatts through February 17, 2027. The company argues that the city is "seeking to regulate energy usage." It says the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission has exclusive authority over that field. It seeks $50,000 in damages. The suit followed the city's May denial of a temporary use permit. The case is ongoing.

shortName: Blocktree Properties, LLC v. Public Utility District No. 2 of Grant Cnty. Washington
citation: Blocktree Props., LLC v. Pub. Util. Dist. No.2 of Grant Cnty., No. 19-35277, 2019 WL 5704281 (9th Cir. Nov. 5, 2019) (mem.), aff'g 380 F. Supp. 3d 1102 (E.D. Wash. 2019).
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: On December 19, 2018, Plaintiffs Blocktree Properties, LLC and other cryptocurrency-mining companies and an individual filed the lawsuit against Public Utility District No.2 of Grant County and its commissioners. The case was filed in the District Court for the Eastern District of Washington. Plaintiffs challenged the District No. 2's new and more expensive "evolving industries" electric rate class, and alleged that it was aimed at cryptocurrency miners and violated federal and Washington law. They asked the Court to enjoin the plan. The district court denied a preliminary injunction and found that Plaintiffs had not shown irreparable harm. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit affirmed the decision. On March 12, 2020, the district court granted in part the defendant's renewed motion for summary judgment and denied Plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment. The case is closed.

shortName: Columbia Riverkeeper v. FERC
citation: Columbia Riverkeeper v. Fed. Energy Regul. Comm'n, No. 26-3332 (9th Cir. filed May 26, 2026).
forum: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
category: Environmental Law: Adequacy of Environmental Review
summary: The Columbia Riverkeeper filed a rehearing request with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) under Part I of the Federal Power Act (FPA) against the authorization and National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) review for the project from Rye Development, acting on behalf of FFP Project 101, LLC.  The primary objective of Rye Development's application was to secure an original major license to construct, operate, and maintain the 1,200-megawatt Goldendale Energy Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Project (Project No. 14861) in Klickitat County, Washington, which media reports state is intended in part to power data centers.  FERC issued a final decision denying the request for a rehearing on January 22, 2026, granting the original license for the Goldendale Project subject to specified conditions. Columbia Riverkeeper appealed that decision to the 9th Circuit on May 26, 2026.

shortName: City of El Dorado v. Protect the Heartland, Inc.
citation: City of El Dorado v. Protect the Heartland, Inc., No. BU-2026-CV-000245 (Kan. Dist. Ct. Butler Cnty. July 14, 2026).

shortName: Citizens for Faquier Cnty. v. Town of Warrenton
citation: Citizens for Fauquier Cnty. v. Town of Warrenton, No. CL22000551-00 (Va. Cir. Ct. Fauquier Cnty. filed Dec. 22, 2022).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: On July 12 and October 14, 2022, Citizens for Fauquier County, an environmental nonprofit, submitted Virginia Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests to the town seeking records related to a permit sought by Amazon to build a 220,000-square-foot data center. However, the town withheld 3,142 pieces of correspondence under the FOIA exemption protecting the “working papers and correspondence” of certain executives. On December 22, 2022, Citizens for Fauquier County sued the Town of Warrenton in Fauquier County Circuit Court, seeking to compel officials to make the correspondence public. On February 7, 2023, the court ruled in favor of the Town of Warrenton, and the plaintiffs filed an appeal in September 2023. On July 30, 2024, the Court of Appeals reversed and sent the case back to the lower court. The Court of Appeals said the lower court erred in permitting the town to claim the exemption for both the mayor and the town manager, and erred in using a sample set of 10 emails selected by the town out of 3,142 emails. The case was remanded to the trial court. In August 2024, the Town Council voted to appeal to the Virginia Supreme Court; however, this appeal was withdrawn after the election of new members to the Town Council. On January 14, 2025, the Town Council voted to release all of the correspondence, except anything protected by attorney-client privilege or related to personnel matters.

shortName: Stewart v. Brown Realty Co. of Rayville, Inc.
citation: Stewart v. Brown Realty Co. of Rayville, No. 50262 (La. Dist. Ct. filed July 9, 2025).
forum: "Fifth Judicial District Court, Richland Parish, Louisiana, Division A"
category: Common Law: Property
summary: On July 9, 2025, Dennis G. Stewart filed a lawsuit in the Fifth Judicial District Court for Richland Parish, Louisiana, against Brown Realty Co. of Rayville, Inc. and several individuals. The plaintiff brought a claim under Louisiana's doctrine of lesion beyond moiety, alleging that the $3,000-per-acre sale price for his Holly Ridge land was less than half its fair market value. The plaintiff further alleged that the buyers, a group of Brown Realty executives and their family members, had access to information that led them to believe the property was more valuable than the purchase price and used it to benefit themselves in violation of their duty to him, and that Brown Realty later advertised nearby tracts for more than ten times what the buyers paid him. The plaintiff sought to unwind the September 2024 sale, which took place months before Meta's nearby data center was publicly announced. The case remains open, and no final decision appears in the available sources.

shortName: Digiport, Inc. v. Foram Dev. BFC, LLC
citation: Digiport, Inc. v. Foram Dev. BFC, LLC, 314 So. 3d 550 (Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 2020)
forum: "District Court of Appeal of Florida, Third District"
category: Corporate: IP
summary: Digiport, a data center development companies brought claims against a data center owner for misappropriation of a trade secret under Florida's Uniform Trade Secret Act (FUTSA). The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of Foram Group, and Digiport appealed. Digiport's alleged trade secret was a design for a single, centralized data center, where tenants could rent space for computer hardware or use cloud computing services. The District Court of Appeal held that questions of facts remained, specifically whether the alleged trade secret qualifies as a trade secret, and on damages.

shortName: Jane Doe v. OnderLaw, LLC and James G. Onder
citation: Doe v. OnderLaw, LLC, No. 26SL-CC07357 (Mo. Cir. Ct., St. Louis Cnty. filed Nov. 5, 2026)
forum: Circuit Court City of St. Louis
category: Corporate Tax, Securities, Employment and Lobbying: Employment
summary: Jim Onder owns OnderLaw, a personal injury law firm, and is developing a data center. Jane Doe worked at OnderLaw and claims the firm demonstrated workers compensation discrimination under Missouri Workers’ Compensation Law by firing her after she sought medical leave for work-related stress, violated the Missouri Whistleblower Protection Act by retaliating against her after she refused to attempt to influence the City Council’s decision on tax breaks for data centers, and that Jim Onder sexually assaulted and committed battery against her on multiple occasions. Doe is seeking relief via actual damages (economic and non-economic), nominal and/or statutory damages, punitive damages, pre- and post-judgment interest at the maximum legal rate, declaratory and injunctive relief, costs of this action and attorneys fees. This case is pending as of November 2026.

shortName: Underwood Family Farm, LLC v. Prince William Cnty.
citation: Underwood Family Farm, LLC v. Prince William Cnty., No. CL24005849-00 (Prince William Cnty. Cir. Ct. Jan. 20, 2026) (denying motion for reconsideration of summary judgment granted to defendant).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Underwood Family Farm and other landowners in the Prince William Digital Gateway data center corridor sued the county in July 2024 over sharply higher real estate assessments after the December 2023 rezoning. They allege the county assessed their parcels based on speculative future use in combination with surrounding land they had not yet sold, that the assessments were arbitrary, capricious, and non-uniform, and that rollback taxes were improperly charged. They seek corrected assessments and refunds. A Prince William Times report describes a ruling by a circuit judge that the Pageland Lane land had in fact been rezoned for data centers even though the developers had not yet bought it, which the paper characterized as adverse to the landowners. The county has discounted the assessments by about 70%, and individual valuation trials could take up to two years.

shortName: Palmer v. Unified Government of Wyandotte Cnty. & Kansas City
citation: Palmer v. Unified Gov't of Wyandotte Cnty. & Kan. City, No. WY-2025-CV-000623 (Kan. Dist. Ct. Wyandotte Cnty. filed July 25, 2025).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Neal Palmer and Haskell Farms, LLC sued the Unified Government over its rezoning for Red Wolf DCD Properties' proposed $12 billion data center. The project would have six buildings totaling 1.8 million square feet on both sides of Parallel Parkway. The plaintiffs say the rezoning from residential to commercial should not have been approved because the applications had "numerous errors and insufficiencies" and did not follow the municipal code. They also claim the review was rushed without enough study of short- and long-term impacts. They further allege that a commissioner was pressured to recuse himself and that Red Wolf organized the withdrawal of signatures from the south-side protest petition. On October 29, 2025, the court denied the government's motion to dismiss the claims about the south tract. The court said the claims about the north tract may go forward once commissioners make a "final decision" on that application. As of June 2026, media reports described the project as stalled by the lawsuit.

shortName: Land use group 1000 Friends of Oregon and local activists filed a lawsuit against the City of Hillsboro and Washington County in order to block property tax breaks for 17 proposed data center applications. Plaintiffs allege that the city improperly issued enterprise zone tax breaks to the developers of each project. The case is ongoing.
citation: 1000 Friends of Or. v. Dias, No. 26CV30954 (Or. Cir. Ct. filed June 22, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: 1000 Friends of Oregon and several individual and organizational co-petitioners filed a Petition for Writ of Review and Complaint for Declaratory and Injunctive Relief against City of Hillsboro officials (Dan Dias, Robby Hammond, City of Hillsboro) and Washington County officials (Eric Olson, Washington County), naming nine data center companies (including NTT Global, Adobe, QTS, CoreWeave, Dropbox, Flexential, and NVIDIA) as "opposite parties." Petitioners allege the City and County exceeded their jurisdiction, failed to follow statutory procedures, made findings unsupported by substantial evidence, and misconstrued Oregon's Enterprise Zone Act (ORS 285C) in approving a batch of Enterprise Zone tax exemption contracts and authorizations — some extending property tax breaks through 2051 — shortly before a new state moratorium (HB 4084) took effect. The petition seeks a writ of review reversing or annulling the challenged contracts and approvals, declaratory relief under Oregon's Uniform Declaratory Judgments Act, and an award of attorney fees.

shortName: Application of Xcel Energy and Otter Tail Power Company for an Energy Facility Permit to Construct the PowerOn Midwest Project
citation: Application of Xcel Energy and Otter Tail Power Company for an Energy Facility Permit to Construct the PowerOn Midwest Project, Docket No. EL26-026 (S.D. Pub. Utils. Comm'n, filed Sept. 4, 2026).
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The South Dakota PUC is considering an application for a 160 miles of new 765 kv transmission lines and multiple substation upgrades from Excel energy called PowerOn Midwest. The need for the new high capacity backbone line is being justified by the applicant based on increasing demand from data centers and industrial projects. Some community members oppose the project and the PUC is currently considering requests for confidential documents to be shared with the public.
secondaryCategory: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions

shortName: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt, LLC v. Bd. of Assessment Appeals
citation: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt, LLC v. Board of Assessment Appeals of Trumbull, 211 Conn. App. 559 (2022), cert. denied, 343 Conn. 926 (2022).
category: Corporate Tax, Securities and Lobbying: Tax
summary: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt LLC, the owner of a data center property in Trumbull, Connecticut, challenged the Town of Trumbull’s property tax assessment of the facility, filing separate tax appeals in the Superior Court, Judicial District of New Britain, for two successive assessment years (Docket Nos. HHBCV146025041S and HHBCV156029300S). On August 4, 2020, the trial court ruled in favor of the property owner, reducing the Town’s valuation of the property by more than $36 million. The Board of Assessment Appeals and the Town of Trumbull appealed to the Connecticut Appellate Court, arguing that the trial court erred in its valuation determination. In a decision issued April 5, 2022, the Appellate Court affirmed the trial court’s judgment. The Town’s petition for certification to the Connecticut Supreme Court was subsequently denied.

citation: Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. submits tariff filing per 35.13(a)(2)(iii): 2026-08-28_Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads
category: Energy Law: RTOs, FERC, DOE
summary: In late August 2026, MISO filed interconnection reliability rules for loads above 50W with FERC.  Dozens of motions to intervene and comments have been submitted to the docket.  The order covers visibility reporting (auditing), grid performance monitoring, ramp rate limits and ride-through requirements to avoid many loads dropping simultaneously. The filing is part of MISO's response to FERC's show-cause order from June 2026.

shortName: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
citation: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin, 2017 WL 11393319 (Tex. Dist. Ct. Nov. 27, 2017), aff’d in part, rev’d in part, & remanded, 575 S.W.3d 92 (Tex. App.—Houston [14th Dist.] 2019), judgment aff’d in part and rev’d in part, 620 S.W.3d 692 (Tex. 2021)
category: Constitutional Law: Takings
summary:
Data Foundry (Plaintiff) operated data centers in Austin, TX, and purchased its electricity from Austin Energy (the sole entity that provides electricity in that municipality and is owned by the City of Austin (Defendant)). Austin Energy proposed a new rate structure; Data Foundry challenged this in administrative hearings, and then sued in court on the basis that the proposed rates were discriminatory and excessive. The city filed a motion to dismiss the case on the basis of Texas Rule 91a (i.e., the claim had no basis in law or fact). The trial court dismissed the case on the basis of Data Foundry lacking standing.
On appeal, the appellate court ruled that Data Foundry had standing because it was being required to pay higher charges, but the court ruled that rate review was not within the jurisdiction of the courts.
On appeal to the Texas Supreme Court, the court ruled that Data Foundry had standing and ordered that the trial court rule on jurisdiction and whether the rates proposed were discriminatory.

shortName: West Buckeye Rd. LP v. City of Phoenix
citation: W. Buckeye Rd. LP v. City of Phoenix, No. CV2026-009522 (Ariz. Super. Ct. Maricopa Cnty. filed Mar. 4, 2026).
forum: Superior Court of Arizona in Maricopa County

summary: The plaintiff, West Buckeye Rd LP filed this lawsuit against the City of Phoenix in the Maricopa County Superior Court. The suit followed the Phoenix City Council's ordinance on Jul. 2, 2025, which restricts where and how data centers can be built. Plaintiff first submitted a notice of claim under Proposition 207, which the Council considered in executive sessions in Nov. 2025 and Jan. 2026. The plaintiff argues that the new rules reduced the market value of its 70-acre property at Buckeye Road and 99th Avenue by more than $54 million. It seeks compensation under Proposition 207. The case is still open as of October 2026.

shortName: Decatur Twp. Civic Council Inc. v. Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Comm'n
citation: Decatur Twp. Civic Council Inc. v. Indianapolis Metro. Dev. Comm'n, No. 49D05-2604-PL-021609 (Ind. Super. Ct. Marion Cnty. filed Apr. 17, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary:
A neighborhood group and seven nearby property owners asked an Indianapolis court to overturn the city's approval of a $4 billion Sabey data center. Decatur Township Civic Council (an Indiana nonprofit) is the first-named petitioner, followed by Timothy W. and Janice F. McWhirter (trustees of their revocable living trust), Charles E. Young II, Leslie Young, Loueva Gay Young, Patricia C. Andrews, and Russell H. Glashan. Each resident petitioner owns or lives on property on Camby Road, Reynolds Road, or Kentucky Avenue in Decatur Township. The suit names five respondents: the Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission (MDC), the City-County Council of Indianapolis, Marion County, Indiana, Sabey Data Center Properties LLC, SCP Decatur Technology Park, L.L.C., and Strategic Capital Partners, LLC. The two SCP/Strategic Capital entities own the land.
The case is a petition for judicial review of a local zoning decision under Indiana law where the petitioners say the decisions were arbitrary, unconstitutional, procedurally improper, and unsupported by substantial evidence, citing Ind. Code § 36-7-4-1614. They also say the variances fail the statutory standards in Ind. Code § 36-7-4-918.4. The petition raises a "disguised rezoning" theory that the variances and commitment changes produced a basic change in use without a new rezoning and City-County Council review under §§ 36-7-4-601 and 608. The petitioners say the changes ignored the comprehensive plan in violation of § 36-7-4-603. They also say the MDC did not follow the commitment rules in § 36-7-4-1015. On constitutional grounds, the petition cites due process under Article I, Section 12 of the Indiana Constitution. A separate declaratory judgment count alleges spot zoning and a violation of the Open Door Law, Ind. Code § 5-14-1.5-3, based on alleged non-public meetings. The variances allow a data center technology park on a site of about 132 acres that is zoned I-2. The petition describes the project as about 250 megawatts and about 1,062,500 square feet of building space. The defendants moved to dismiss on June 15, 2026, arguing that the petition "fails to comply with all statutory requirements" for judicial review. The judge has not ruled on the motion to dismiss yet.

forum: United States District Court for the Western District of Washington
category: Corporate Tax, Securities, Employment and Lobbying: Employment
summary: The plaintiff, a data center technician, sued his data center employer, alleging violations of state and federal employment laws. Plaintiff claimed that his sleep apnea made him unable to meet his on-call responsibilities, and request accomodation. Defendant, which operates data centers in Washington, decided that it could not reasonably accomodate plaintiff's condition, and placed him on unpaid leave. The court held that on-call rotations were an essential responsibility, and that the plaintiff was not entitled to accomodation.

shortName: In re NorthWestern Energy's Provision of Electricity Supply Service to Data Centers
citation: In re NorthWestern Energy's Provision of Electricity Supply Service to Data Centers, No. 2025.11.084 (Mont. Pub. Serv. Comm'n filed Nov. 17, 2025).
summary: On November 17, 2025, nine environmental, community, and public-interest organizations filed a complaint with the Montana Public Service Commission challenging NorthWestern Energy's proposed electricity supply service for large data centers. The proceeding concerns Montana public utility regulation under Mont. Code Ann. §§ 69-8-201(1) and 69-3-321(1), including regulatory oversight, tariff requirements, and protection of existing customers from infrastructure costs associated with large electricity loads. Complainants allege that NorthWestern entered into preliminary agreements to supply up to 1,400 megawatts of electricity to three data centers without first demonstrating that the arrangements would not adversely affect existing ratepayers or providing sufficient information for public review. They seek a contested proceeding, a separate data center customer classification and tariff, and safeguards preventing the allocation of data center-related costs to existing customers. NorthWestern moved to dismiss the complaint in February 2026, arguing that no data center had begun purchasing electricity supply service and that the claims were premature. As of October 20, 2026, there has been no final decision.

shortName: Soriano v. City of Hobart Plan Comm'n
citation: Soriano v. City of Hobart Plan Commission, No. 45D11-2512-MI-000644 (Lake Super. Ct. filed Dec. 8, 2025).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Angelita Soriano, Joseph Conn, Barbara Koteles, and Albina Venegas-Roman filed a verified complaint against the City of Hobart Plan Commission and the Common Council of the City of Hobart in Lake Superior Court on December 8, 2025, challenging the city’s approval of a fill permit for a proposed Amazon data center project. The plaintiffs contend that the city failed to follow procedural requirements under state law, including holding a public information meeting for residents, before granting the approval. Hobart Owner LLC, Tuhaus LLC, and Amazon Data Services, Inc. later intervened in support of the defendants. In July 2026, the court consolidated this case with a related proceeding, Docket No. 45D10-2606-RA-00007, which the parties and the court have since referred to as “Soriano II.” On October 15, 2026, the court granted a motion to dismiss Soriano II with prejudice, finding that those plaintiffs had failed to timely file the administrative record required under Indiana’s Administrative Orders and Procedures Act, though it remains unclear whether this ruling resolved the claims brought by the plaintiffs named in this docket. The case remains pending until October 2026.

citation: Newson-Pace v. HITT Contracting Inc., No. 3:25-cv-00197 (N.D. Ga. dismissed Feb. 11, 2026) (voluntary dismissal).
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia
category: Corporate Tax, Securities, Employment and Lobbying: Employment
summary: Alton R Matthews, Charlie Williams, and Cheree Newson-Pace filed suit against HITT Contracting INC., SAVI EHS/Amphibious Group, Brigada Co, and Certified Safety Experts in the Superior Court of Fayette County, Georgia, on August 7, 2025. The case was later removed to the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, Newnan Division. The plaintiffs were safety managers at a data center project in Fayetteville and alleged they suffered wrongful termination, retaliation, blacklisting, and labor violations after raising concerns related to unsafe practices in the workplace. The case was terminated on February 11, 2026, after a voluntary dismissal filed by the plaintiffs.

summary: Layne Thornton and his Toledo Dairy Corporation petitioned for judicial review following the Kuna City Council's approval of a rezone for Diode Ventures' 620-acre, $1 billion Gemstone Technology Park data center campus. Plaintiffs argue that council member Greg McPherson should have recused himself from the vote; McPherson was employed by Thornton at the time, and Thornton's property directly bordered the proposed data center site. The District Court denied Thornton's petition, and Thornton appealed to the Idaho Supreme Court in June 2026.

forum: Superior Court of New Jersey Law Division: Somerset County
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: 1200 Route 22 Land Investors, a data center developer, sued the the Township of Bridgewater and its Planning Board, challenging a newly adopted ordinance imposing additional regulations on data centers. The ordinance would require data centers to adopt closed-loop cooling systems and heat-recovery technology. The plaintiff alleges that the ordinance violates an existing redevelopment plan that permits building data centers on its property.

shortName: Public Utility Comm'n of Texas v. Paxton
citation: Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex. v. Paxton, No. D-1-GN-25-004622 (Tex. Dist. Ct. Travis Cnty. filed June 27, 2025).
forum: "District Court of Texas, 419th Judicial District, Travis County"
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: On June 27, 2025, the Public Utility Commission of Texas sued Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in Travis County District Court, seeking a declaratory judgment to clarify the Texas Public Information Act and block the disclosure of information on cryptocurrency mining. In 2023, the Texas Legislature passed Senate Bill 1929, which requires cryptocurrency mining facilities using an electrical load over 75 megawatts to register with the Public Utility Commission by 2025. When reporters from Straight Arrow News and The Texas Tribune made a public information request to the Public Utility Commission for the specifics—name, location, and electrical load—of the cryptocurrency facilities, the request was denied. In February 2025, the reporters brought the matter to the Texas Attorney General’s office, which ruled in May that some of the information should be released. This led to the lawsuit brought by the Public Utility Commission, based on the claim that disclosure of the information on the crypto facilities was not permitted under the Texas Public Information Act because it could aid potential terrorists in acts against the Texas energy grid. On September 16, 2025, Texas Democracy Foundation joined the defendant as an intervenor, followed by the Texas Tribune on October 23, 2025. The case has not been ruled on and remains pending.

shortName: BladeRoom Group Ltd. v. Facebook, Inc.
citation: BladeRoom Group Limited v. Facebook, Inc.
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of California
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: BladeRoom Group and an affiliate sued Facebook, Emerson Electric, and related Emerson entities in 2015, alleging that after BladeRoom pitched its modular data center design to Facebook under a non-disclosure agreement in 2011–2012, Facebook and Emerson conspired to misappropriate BladeRoom's trade secrets to build Facebook's Luleå, Sweden data center, and that Facebook then shared the design through the Open Compute Project without authorization. BladeRoom's claims included breach of the NDA, misappropriation of trade secrets, unjust enrichment, and unfair competition, and it originally sought roughly $365 million in damages. Facebook settled with BladeRoom during trial for a reported $365 million; the case proceeded to a jury verdict against Emerson alone, which found willful and malicious trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract and awarded roughly $30 million in compensatory damages (later increased with exemplary damages and prejudgment interest to over $77 million) — a judgment the Ninth Circuit later vacated in part on appeal, remanding for further proceedings regarding the NDA's expiration date.

shortName: NDNB Assurance, LLP v. Giga Data Center-1 LLC
citation: NDNB Assur., LLP v. Giga Data Ctr.-1 LLC, No. 1:26-cv-00129 (N.D. Ga. dismissed Jan. 26, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia
category: Arbitration
summary: NDNB Assurance, LLP filed suit against Gigadata Center1LLC (a Delaware LLC), and Gigadata Centers LLC (a Georgia LLC) in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia on January 9, 2026. Under the Federal Arbitration Act, the plaintiff filed a motion to confirm an arbitral award in the Arbitration Proceeding Case No. 01-22-0003-3283. In that case, the plaintiff was awarded the amount of $126,805.75 but alleges that the defendants did not make any payment. The court ordered the plaintiff to present a supplemental filing providing sufficient grounds to justify the court's jurisdiction. The matter was dismissed without prejudice on January 26, 2026, because of the plaintiff's failure to obey the order of the court.

shortName: RD Michigan Property Owner I, LLC v. Saline Twp.
citation: RD Mich. Prop. Owner I LLC v. Saline Township, No. 25-001577-CZ (Mich. Cir. Ct. Washtenaw Cnty. Oct. 15, 2025) (consent judgment).
corporateEntities: Related Digital; OpenAI and Oracle’s Stargate
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: The developer Related Digital and the site's landowners sued Saline Township after the township board voted 4-1 to deny a conditional rezoning for the data center. Their legal theory was exclusionary zoning under Michigan law, meaning that the township had unreasonably barred a legitimate land use. The township settled, and the court entered a consent judgment on October 15, 2025, that allows the project to proceed. Under the settlement, the township receives about $14 million in community benefits. The developer also agreed to limit water use and noise. A local resident, Kathryn Haushalter, later tried to intervene in the closed case, arguing that the township violated the Open Meetings Act by not voting in public to settle. She also argued that the consent judgment authorized a type of conditional rezoning that the township's own ordinance forbids. The court rejected the open-meetings claim, noting that there was a public comment period and a public motion to approve the judgment, and it denied her motion to intervene as untimely. On April 28, 2026, the Court of Appeals dismissed her appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

shortName: State ex rel. McNamara-Smith v. Grube
citation: State ex rel. McNamara-Smith v. Grube, Slip Op. No. 2026-Ohio-3035
category: Information/Records Requests/Elections and Ballot Measures
summary: In April 2026, the Ashville, OH Village Council issued a resolution approving a development and supply commitment with EdgeConnex for a data center using emergency powers. Residents of the resolution created a referendum opposing the decision and obtained enough signatures to submit it to the fiscal officer who declined to add it to the ballot due to the use of emergency powers for the resolution. The Ohio Supreme court ruled the resolution did not sufficiently justify the use of emergency powers to avoid consideration of the referendum by the board of elections.

shortName: Thor Equities, LLC v. City of Urbana, Ohio
citation: Thor Equities, LLC v. City of Urbana, No. 3:26-cv-00196 (S.D. Ohio filed June 19, 2026).
forum: United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio
category: Constitutional Law: Due Process
summary: Thor Equities, LLC, Urbana Owner LLC, Urbana Owner I LLC, Urbana Owner LLC, and Highland55 Investments LLC filed suit against the City of Urbana, Ohio, its city council, and building and zoning appeals board in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. The plaintiff, a data center developer, sought a declaratory judgment and preliminary and permanent injunction relief regarding the denial of the plaintiff's site plan application to develop a data center in the city and a 12-month moratorium for data center construction approved by the defendants. The plaintiff Thor, alleges that it has invested millions of dollars in a data center project in the city, claims that this moratorium is illegal, and that the defendants had no legal authority to proceed with it. In addition, the plaintiff requested compensation for damages to be determined by the jury. No final decision has been issued yet.

forum: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas
category: Corporate: IP

shortName: Kentucky Industrial Alliance, LLC v. City of Cave City
citation: Ky. Indus. All., LLC v. City of Cave City, No. 26-CI-00445 (Ky. Cir. Ct. Barren Cnty. filed June 8, 2026).
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: Kentucky Industrial Alliance (KIA) sued Cave City, its city council, and the Joint City-County Planning Commission. KIA planned to build a 600-acre, 1.2-gigawatt AI and cloud computing campus (including a development plan for 2001 Doyle Avenue). The site sits near I-65 and close to Mammoth Cave National Park. On May 18, 2026 the city council enacted a 12-month moratorium on data center applications. KIA has asked the court to declare the moratorium unlawful. The company says it filed a preliminary development plan application on May 11, 2026, just before the moratorium. It wants that application reviewed under the zoning rules in place at the time of filing. The verified complaint says the moratorium violates KRS Chapter 100 and interferes with the company's vested rights. It also claims the city skipped required planning, notice, and public hearing procedures. The city moved to dismiss for lack of standing, arguing that the company's application papers were incomplete. The company filed a second suit, No. 26-CI-00500, to void the city's 2024 annexation of the property. On August 24, 2026, Judge John T. Alexander's court agreed to consolidate the two cases. The consolidated cases are due back in court November 23, 2026.

citation: Kanter v. O’Leary, 2:26-cv-00664 (D. Utah filed July 15, 2026)
category: Common Law: Torts

shortName: Travelers Property Casualty Co. of America v. Rosendin Electric Inc.
citation: Travelers Prop. Cas. Co. of Am. v. Rosendin Elec., Inc., No. 2:20-cv-00130 (D. Ariz. Filed Jan. 16, 2020).
forum: United States District Court for the District of Arizona
category: Common Law: Contract Disputes Among Developers
summary: On January 16, 2020, Travelers Property Casualty Company of America (“Plaintiff”), an insurance company, sued Rosendin Electric, Inc. (“REI”) and DPR Construction (“DPR”) in the United States District Court for the District of Arizona. DPR entered into a written contract with REI for the latter to perform electrical work on the Aligned Energy MEP West data center project in Phoenix, Arizona.  Plaintiff issued a commercial general liability policy to defendant DPR in which Plaintiff agreed to pay sums that the insured becomes legally obligated to pay as damages because of property damage caused by an occurrence not otherwise excluded or barred. DPR was sued in Arizona State Court in Maricopa County by Aligned Data Centers Propco, LLC for damages alleged to have been caused in connection with a power outage at the data center allegedly caused by work REI was performing under DPR’s supervision. Plaintiff seeks a declaratory judgment and contends that DPR’s insurance claims filed in association with the power outage are not covered under the insurance policy and that Plaintiff does not owe an obligation to defend nor indemnify DPR and REI. On April 10, 2020, the case was dismissed pursuant to FRCP 41 without prejudice.

shortName: Appalachian Voices v. Tennessee Valley Authority
citation: Appalachian Voices v. Tenn. Valley Auth., No. 3:26-cv-01279 (M.D. Tenn. filed Sept. 8, 2026)
forum: United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee
category: Environmental Law: Pollution Control
summary: The plaintiff environmental advocacy organizations sued TVA for renegging on a plan to retire a coal plant during the construction of a replacement gas plant potentially in violation of major source air pollution limitations. Plaintiffs are seeking a declaratory judgment that TVA is violating the Clean Air Act and an injunction against further violations.

shortName: 1778 Rich Pike LLC v. Clifton Twp. Zoning
citation: 1778 Rich Pike LLC v. Clifton Twp. Zoning Hearing Bd., No. 2025-09492 (Lackawanna Cnty. Ct. Com. Pl. filed Dec. 1, 2025)
forum: "Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas, Lackawanna County"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: 1778 Rich Pike, LLC, filed a land use appeal against the Clifton Township Zoning Hearing Board in the Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas, Lackawanna County, in December 2025. This appeal follows the zoning board’s denial of 1778 Rich Pike’s substantive validity challenge (filed April 2025, denied November 2025) to the Clifton Township Zoning Ordinance, which alleged that pursuant to the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code, the Clifton Township Ordinance unlawfully banned data centers. In January 2026, 1778 Rich Pike and the Township reached a settlement that would allow 1778 Rich Pike to build a data center on their property without a conditional use agreement. A neighboring township, Covington, then petitioned the court to intervene because it alleged that the settlement would lead to the county having to build more infrastructure such as power stations, water wells, and sewage treatment. The Court vacated the settlement on January 30, 2026. The case is pending as of October 2026.

shortName: In re Evergy Kansas Metro, Inc.
citation: In re Application of Evergy Kansas Metro, Inc., Docket No. 25-EKME-315-TAR (Kan. Corp. Comm’n filed Feb. 11, 2025).
summary: Evergy Metro, Inc., a public utility company, filed an Application for approval of Evergy’s Large Load Power Service Rate Plan and Associated Tariffs with the State Corporation Commission of the State of Kansas. The Commission, after negotiation with interested parties, reached a settlement on a new rate plan designed to serve electric customers requiring greater than 75 megawatts of peak power consumption, particularly data centers. The plan requires its users to pay a minimum monthly bill based on 80% of their contract demand, regardless of actual usage. It also assigns an early termination fee and infrastructure construction costs to its users.

shortName: Franklin Citizens for Responsible Development, Inc. v. City of Franklin Planning & Zoning Comm'n
citation: Franklin Citizens for Responsible Dev., Inc. v. City of Franklin Plan. & Zoning Comm'n, No. 26-CI-00123 (Ky. Cir. Ct. Simpson Cnty. filed Apr. 2, 2026).
corporateEntities: Tenkey Landco I, LLC; SPDJ Partners, LLC; OTN Development Company, LLC; “Project Lionsgate/Blackjack”
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Substantive Planning Decisions
summary: A nonprofit citizens' group, Franklin Citizens for Responsible Development, filed suit on April 2, 2026 asking for a declaratory judgment overturning the March 3 approval of a preliminary development plan for TenKey LandCo's data center. TenKey plans an AI data center campus with onsite power generation on 200 acres near I-65. The group argues that the commission had no authority to approve the plan, because in 2025 it had found the project was not a permitted use and said such projects should go through the conditional use process. The complaint calls the approval "arbitrary, capricious, and inconsistent with the City of Franklin Zoning Ordinance." It also raises noise, light, air emissions, and strain on water and other local resources. TenKey and the commission moved to dismiss, arguing that the group lacks standing under a 2025 amendment to Kentucky law. The group argues that the narrower standing rule, enacted through House Bill 321, is unconstitutional. Judge Mark Thurmond heard arguments on July 20. The decision on the motions is still pending.

shortName: Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana v. Duke Energy Indiana
citation: Citizens Action Coalition of Ind. v. Duke Energy Ind., No. 26S-EX-127 (Ind. argued Sept. 17, 2026).
summary: This Indiana Supreme Court case is focused on associational standing. The underlying case involves the Indiana Utilities Regulatory Commission's approval of two gas plants proposed by Duke Energy under a pay-as-you build approach.  Citizens Action Coalition and Vote Solar challenged the decision in court and Duke responded by petitioning the Indiana Supreme Court to rule on the associational standing issue.

shortName: Oregon Environmental Council v. IRS
citation: Or. Env't Council v. IRS, 836 F. Supp. 3d 1 (D.D.C. 2026)
forum: "United States District Court, District of Columbia"
category: Corporate: Tax
summary: Organization representing energy consumers in Oregon and environmental advocacy group brought action against InternalRevenue Service challenging as arbitrary and capricious under Administrative Procedure Act the IRS notice that eliminated 5% safe harbor method for establishing “beginning of construction,” as eligibility criteria for wind and large solar projects to receive expiring clean electricity tax credits. The parties filed a cross motion for summary judgment. The District Court held that the consumer and environmental organizations had associational standing, granted the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment, vacated the IRS's notice, and remanded for further administrative actions.

shortName: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg Cnty. v. Valara Holdings, LLC
citation: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg Cnty. v. Valara Holdings, LLC, No. 2026-CP-42-03416 (S.C. Ct. Com. Pl. dismissed Oct. 6, 2026), appeal docketed (S.C. Ct. App. filed Oct. 20, 2026).
forum: Spartanburg County Court of Common Pleas
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg County, a group of area residents represented by the South Carolina Environmental Law Center, filed suit against Valara Holdings, LLC, Spartanburg County, and the Spartanburg County Administrator in the Spartanburg County Court of Common Pleas on July 6, 2026. The plaintiffs allege that a proposed data center project was improperly split into two applications and classified as a “minor” land development under the County’s Unified Land Management Ordinance, allowing the project to bypass the public review process required for a “major” development. The plaintiffs sought a declaration that the project should have been classified as major and asked the court to require major-development review, and they later moved for a preliminary injunction and for summary judgment. The defendants moved to dismiss the action, and on October 6, 2026, the court granted dismissal. The plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal to the South Carolina Court of Appeals on October 20, 2026.

shortName: Piatt v. City of Granbury
citation: Piatt v. City of Granbury, No. C2026159 (335th Dist. Ct., Hood Cnty., Tex. filed Apr. 6, 2026).
forum: "355th Judicial District Court of Texas, Hood County"
category: Land Use Planning and Zoning: Public Meeting and Notice Requirements
summary: Daniel Piatt, Janet Logsdon, James Logsdon, and Craig Jackson, all residents, taxpayers, and property owners in Granbury and Hood County, Texas, filed this action against the City of Granbury, Mayor Jim Jarratt, Mayor Pro Tem Bruce Wadley, four City Council members, and the City Manager in the 335th Judicial District Court of Hood County on April 6, 2026. The plaintiffs alleged that the City Council violated the Texas Open Meetings Act in connection with its approval of the annexation of a roughly 2,098-acre property known as Knox Ranch, which the plaintiffs contend was intended for a data center development. The petition alleges that a majority of the Council toured a facility operated by Bilateral Energy without proper public notice, describing this as a walking quorum, and that the annexation service plan was not made available to the public before the Council’s vote. The plaintiffs seek a declaratory judgment that the Council’s approval is void or voidable, along with a temporary restraining order and a permanent injunction barring the defendants from proceeding with the annexation and related agreements. This case remains pending as of October 2026.
